label: Chapter 7 · Part B
title: Common Objections II: Scientism, Other Gods, Evil & Hiddenness
tagline: Why “science says no,” “one god further,” and even suffering do not overturn the proofs
oneSentence: The most popular modern objections to natural theology — scientism, brute-fact laws, the “complex designer,” “one god further,” the gap between the philosophers’ God and the believer’s, evil, hiddenness, suspect motives, and persistent disagreement — either refute themselves, attack a caricature of classical theism, or hold the proofs to a standard nobody applies elsewhere, so none of them touches the five demonstrations.
bigPicture:
This module covers the second half of Feser’s final chapter, where he turns from technical objections to the cosmological argument (Part A) to the broad, culturally dominant reasons people give for dismissing natural theology without examining it. The centerpiece is a long critique of **scientism** — the view that science is the only genuine source of knowledge. Feser treats it at length because it is the unspoken premise behind most New Atheist objections: if only science counts as knowledge, then metaphysical demonstrations can be waved away as unscientific before anyone reads them.

Against scientism Feser presses four problems: it is self-refuting or else trivial; the method of physics cannot in principle give a complete description even of physical reality; the laws of nature that science appeals to cannot be the ultimate explanation of anything; and the main argument for scientism — the predictive and technological success of science — simply does not support it. He then works through eight further objections: that the fundamental laws are a brute fact; that a designer would be more complex than the universe; that theists should go “one god further” and reject their God as they reject Zeus; that the philosophers’ God is not the God of ordinary believers; the problem of evil (both Mackie’s logical version and Rowe’s evidential version); divine hiddenness; the charge that theistic arguments are mere rationalizations; and the claim that no one can have a proof when so many people remain unconvinced.

What unifies the section is a diagnostic pattern worth mastering. Nearly every objection does one of three things: it saws off the branch it sits on (scientism, Hume’s Fork); it attacks a picture of God as one more complex being or hypothesis inside the universe rather than the purely actual, simple, necessary source of all being that the five proofs actually conclude to (the complex designer, one god further, brute-fact laws); or it evaluates strict demonstrations by the wrong standards — probability, parsimony, universal assent, the motives of the arguer. Once you can spot which move is being made, you can answer most popular objections briefly and calmly.

The section is also where the book faces the hardest emotional objection — suffering. Feser offers a **defense** rather than a full **theodicy**: he argues that evil is logically compatible with God and that, given independent proof that God exists and is good, we have reason to think a greater good is drawn from evil even when we cannot see it. For someone who wants to persuade, this is the most delicate ground in the whole course, and this module pays special attention to answering it humanely rather than glibly. The chapter — and the book — ends with Feser’s account of what “demonstration” means and his conclusion that the five proofs stand.
objectives: State the four problems Feser raises against scientism and explain why the first one makes scientism either self-refuting or vacuous.
Use the airplane-engineer and metal-detector analogies to show why the success of physics does not show that physics describes all of reality.

Explain why no account of the “laws of nature” (Aristotelian, Cartesian-Newtonian, Humean, Platonic) lets laws serve as the ultimate explanation of the world, and why treating them as a brute fact fails.
Explain why Hume’s and Dawkins’ “complex designer” objection misses arguments that conclude to an absolutely simple first cause.
Diagnose the “one god further” objection as a category mistake, using the triangularity or Form-of-the-Good analogy.
Distinguish a defense from a theodicy and the logical from the evidential problem of evil, and reconstruct Feser’s replies to Mackie and to Rowe.
Identify the two assumptions behind the divine hiddenness argument and give Feser’s reasons for rejecting each.
Explain what classical theists mean by a “demonstration,” and why controversy or suspect motives do not show that a demonstration fails.
Give a crisp, calm one-line answer to each objection, and respond to someone in real pain over suffering without being glib.

summary.heading: Scientism: the hidden premise and its four problems
summary.body:
The first objection in this half of the chapter is the one Feser treats at greatest length: the claim that science is the only genuine source of knowledge, and that since our best scientific theories nowhere mention God, belief in God has no rational standing. Feser calls the underlying view **scientism** — the thesis that science alone gives us knowledge, so that any philosophy or metaphysics worth taking seriously is simply whatever is already implicit in science. It is a central ingredient of the New Atheism, and Alex Rosenberg, whom Feser quotes repeatedly, openly embraces the label.

Why spend so long on it? Because scientism is what allows critics to dismiss natural theology without reading it. If only science counts as knowledge, then metaphysical demonstrations are ruled out in advance as “unscientific,” and no one needs to check their premises. Feser’s verdict is blunt: despite the confidence of its advocates, there are no good arguments for scientism at all and there are decisive arguments against it.

He announces four problems before examining each in turn:

1. Scientism is self-defeating, and it can avoid that only by becoming trivial.
2. Scientific method cannot even in principle give a complete description of reality — not even of physical reality.
3. The laws of nature by which science explains things cannot in principle provide a complete explanation of reality.
4. The main argument for scientism — the predictive and technological success of modern science — has no force.

The order matters. The first problem attacks scientism’s logical coherence; the second and third show that even if we set coherence aside, science by its very method leaves things out, both in what it can describe and in what it can explain; the fourth removes the chief reason people give for believing scientism anyway.
summary.takeaway: Scientism — the claim that only science gives knowledge — is the hidden premise that lets critics dismiss natural theology unread, so Feser attacks it on four fronts: coherence, description, explanation, and its supporting argument.
summary.deepDive:
The first thing to get clear is the difference between **science** and **scientism**. Science is a family of methods — observation, controlled experiment, mathematical modeling — for studying the measurable, predictable features of nature. Scientism is not one more such method. It is a claim *about* all methods: that only these ones yield knowledge. That claim is philosophical, which is why Feser can criticize it without criticizing a single scientific result. People often think that to reject scientism is to be suspicious of science; but Feser praises physics throughout this section, and the five proofs never contradict any scientific finding.

Notice also how the objection is worded: our best scientific theories make no reference to God. Taken alone that observation is harmless. Our best theories also make no reference to justice, to the meaning of a sentence, or to the truth of the law of non-contradiction — yet no one concludes these are unreal. The observation becomes an argument against God only when joined to scientism: if science doesn’t mention it and science is the only source of knowledge, we can’t know it. So the whole objection rides on the scientism premise. Remove that premise and “science doesn’t mention God” is about as significant as “chemistry doesn’t mention sonnets.”

A worked example helps. Imagine someone who says, “The only reliable way to know what’s in a room is to use a thermometer; thermometers never register chairs; so there are no chairs.” The failure is obvious because we can see that thermometers are built to register only one thing. Feser’s strategy is to make the same limitation visible for science — first by showing that the thesis of scientism cannot pass its own test (steps 1–7 of the module’s argument), then by showing the built-in limits of scientific description and explanation (steps 8–14), and finally by exposing the inference from science’s success to its completeness (steps 15–19).

One nuance: Feser is not claiming that philosophy competes with science on science’s own ground. His point is that there are questions — about what science presupposes, how its results should be interpreted, and what ultimately explains the laws it uses — that science by its nature cannot answer. The five proofs live precisely there, which is why removing scientism (step 19) leaves the critic with no shortcut past them (step 20).

checks.q: Why does Feser devote so much space to scientism in particular?
options: Because it is the most technical objection to the Aristotelian proof
Because it is the premise that lets critics dismiss natural theology without examining its arguments
Because most atheists explicitly defend it in print
Because it was the main objection raised by Hume
checks.explanation: Scientism rules natural theology out in advance as unscientific. Remove it and the critic must actually engage the proofs.

checks.q: Which of the following is NOT one of Feser’s four problems with scientism?
options: It is self-refuting or trivial
Science cannot give a complete description of reality
The argument from science’s success has no force
Scientific theories are too often revised to be trusted
checks.explanation: Feser never argues from the revisability or unreliability of science. His four problems concern coherence, description, explanation, and the success argument.

checks.q: Why is the observation that “our best scientific theories make no reference to God” not by itself an argument against God?
options: Because it only gains force when combined with the premise that science is the only source of knowledge
Because some scientific theories do mention God
Because scientists privately believe in God
Because theories can be revised to include God later
checks.explanation: Science also doesn’t mention justice or logical truths. The observation becomes an objection only with scientism added.

summary.plain: Many people think science is the only way to really know anything, and since science never mentions God, they figure there’s nothing to discuss. Feser thinks this belief — he calls it “scientism” — is the hidden reason people ignore arguments for God. He says it has four big problems, and he goes through them one by one.

summary.heading: Problem 1: self-refuting or trivial
summary.body:
The first horn of the dilemma: the claim that science’s methods are the only reliable route to knowledge (Feser cites Alex Rosenberg’s formulation) is not itself a scientific result. No experiment establishes it. In fact, not even the claim that science is *a* rational form of inquiry can be established scientifically, because science rests on philosophical presuppositions: that there is an objective world outside scientists’ minds; that this world has regularities that laws could capture; that our intellects and senses can discover and describe those regularities. Science presupposes these, so it cannot justify them without arguing in a circle. To justify them you must step outside science — and the existence of such an extrascientific standpoint refutes the thesis that only science gives rational access to reality.

Philosophy has also always been needed to *interpret* science: whether the world is made of substances or events, what a cause is, what the universals named in laws (electron, quark) are, and whether theories describe reality at all or are just tools for prediction. Science can shed light on these questions but cannot settle them. Since science depends on philosophy both to justify its starting points and to interpret its results, scientism is doubly false; Feser endorses John Kekes’ verdict that philosophy is a better candidate than science for the model of rationality.

The second horn: the defender of scientism may dig in and say philosophy must therefore be part of science. But then “science” has been redefined to include anything that could be offered against scientism, and the thesis becomes empty. Worse, it becomes consistent with views it was meant to exclude. Aristotle and Aquinas regarded natural theology itself as a science — not mathematical or experimental like physics, but *more* certain than physics, because it rests on strict demonstrations from premises any physical science must assume. If “science” is stretched that far, there is no non-arbitrary way to exclude natural theology. The whole point of invoking scientism was to dismiss natural theology without engaging it; stretched, scientism can no longer do that, and the critic must face the arguments head-on instead of plugging his ears.
summary.takeaway: Taken strictly, scientism is a non-scientific claim that science cannot justify, so it refutes itself; taken broadly enough to include philosophy, it becomes empty and can no longer exclude natural theology.
summary.deepDive:
The hardest idea here is the **circularity** at the base of science. Try a thought experiment. Suppose you want to prove, scientifically, that experiments tell us about a real world outside our minds. You design an experiment, run it, and look at the result. But to treat that result as information about the world, you must already assume that your instruments and senses are putting you in touch with a mind-independent reality that behaves regularly. Whatever outcome you get, you interpret it using the very assumptions you set out to prove. The same goes for the assumption that nature is orderly enough for laws to capture, and for the assumption that the human intellect can grasp that order. These are presuppositions (step 3), not results.

This does not mean science is unreliable. Feser’s point is subtler: science’s reliability, if we know it, is known *from outside science* — by philosophical reflection on knowledge, perception, and the world. And the existence of that outside standpoint is exactly what scientism denies. So the thesis undercuts itself (step 4). Notice too that the thesis “only science yields knowledge” is not itself an experimental finding (step 2); nobody has measured it.

Feser adds a second dependence (step 5): science needs philosophy to *interpret* what it finds. Are there substances, or only events? What is causation? Do the universals named in laws — electron, quark — exist over and above individual particles? Are theories true descriptions or merely predictive instruments? Scientific findings bear on these questions but cannot settle them. That is why Feser endorses Kekes’ judgment that philosophy has the better claim to be the paradigm of rationality.

Now the second horn (step 6). A defender might say, “Fine — philosophy is really part of science.” But then “science” just means “rational inquiry,” and the thesis says nothing more than “only rational inquiry yields knowledge.” Worse, natural theology now qualifies. Aristotle and Aquinas called it a *science* in the older sense of *scientia* — knowledge demonstrated from principles — and held it more certain than physics, because its premises are the very things physics has to take for granted.

People often think this dilemma is a mere debating trick. It isn’t. It shows that scientism cannot do the job it was hired for: justifying the refusal to examine natural theology (step 7). Either the tool breaks (self-refutation) or it becomes too blunt to cut anything (triviality). In both cases, the critic is back to having to engage the arguments.

checks.q: Why can science not justify its own presuppositions (an objective world, regularities, reliable faculties)?
options: Because scientists have not yet run the right experiments
Because those presuppositions are false
Because any scientific attempt to justify them would already assume them, arguing in a circle
Because philosophy forbids it
checks.explanation: Every experiment already presupposes these things, so appealing to experiment to prove them is circular (step 3).

checks.q: What does Feser mean by saying the falsity of scientism is “doubly assured”?
options: Science depends on philosophy both to justify its presuppositions and to interpret its results
Two different scientists have refuted it
It is both self-refuting and immoral
It fails both in physics and in biology
checks.explanation: Philosophy is needed at both ends of science — before (presuppositions) and after (interpretation).

checks.q: A scientism defender says, “Philosophy is just part of science, so scientism stands.” According to Feser, what follows?
options: Scientism becomes a stronger thesis
Philosophy must adopt experimental methods
Natural theology is refuted
The thesis becomes trivial and can no longer exclude natural theology, which Aristotle and Aquinas considered a science
checks.explanation: This is the second horn: a “science” broad enough to include philosophy has no principled way to exclude natural theology.

summary.plain: Here’s the first problem: the claim “only science gives real knowledge” can’t itself be proven by science — no experiment could show it. Science also has to assume some things it can’t test, like that there’s a real world out there. So either the claim defeats itself, or you stretch the word “science” so far that it includes philosophy — and then it can’t be used to rule out arguments for God anymore.

summary.heading: Problem 2: science cannot give a complete description of reality
summary.body:
Paradoxically, the very method that makes physics so successful guarantees its incompleteness. Physics describes the world in purely quantitative terms — following Galileo’s image of nature as a book written in mathematics. So of course it discovers the aspects of reality that can be predicted and controlled: those are the only aspects it allows itself to attend to. Everything else slips through its methodological net.

Ordinary experience is qualitative through and through: colors, sounds, tastes, smells, warmth, pains, thoughts, choices, purposes, meanings. Physics abstracts from all that. There is nothing wrong with abstraction as long as we remember we are doing it. Feser’s illustration: engineers working out how many passengers of average weight a plane can carry ignore everything about people except weight — and even ignore actual weights in favor of an average no real person may have. Very useful. But it would be absurd for the people planning in-flight meals and movies to rely only on the engineers’ data, and more absurd to insist that because the data say nothing about food or film preferences, there are no such preferences. The data are silent *because* the method guaranteed they would be.

Physics is no less abstract. If some familiar feature of the world doesn’t appear in physics, that is not a discovery that it isn’t there; the method stipulated in advance that it be left out. Feser recalls Bertrand Russell — no friend of natural theology — who stressed that physics gives only the abstract, mathematical structure of events and says nothing of the intrinsic character of whatever has that structure. And that means physics itself implies there is more to reality than it describes, because there cannot be a structure without something that has the structure.
summary.takeaway: Physics describes only the mathematically modelable structure of nature, leaving everything else out by design — so its silence about a feature is no evidence the feature is absent, and its structural description itself implies there is more to reality.
summary.deepDive:
Start with the paradox Feser flags: the very method that makes physics so powerful guarantees its incompleteness. Physics decides in advance to describe the world quantitatively — Galileo’s book of nature written in mathematics. That decision is what allows precise prediction and technological control (step 8). But it also means that whatever cannot be put into equations is never looked at in the first place.

Feser’s airplane example contains two distinct absurdities, and it is worth separating them. The first would be for the catering staff to rely *only* on the engineers’ data when planning meals. The second, worse one would be to insist that since the data say nothing about food preferences, there is *no fact of the matter* about what passengers like. The second absurdity is the one scientism commits (step 9): it treats silence built into a method as a discovery about the world.

The Russell point (step 10) is harder and deserves a worked example. Think of a chess game recorded in notation: 1. e4 e5 2. Nf3 Nc6. The notation captures the game’s structure perfectly — which piece moved where, in what order. But it is completely silent about what the pieces are: carved wood, plastic, people standing on a giant lawn, or bits in a computer. The same structure can be realized by very different stuff. Now, a record of moves without anything that moves is not a game at all; there must be *something* standing in those relations. Russell says physics is like the notation: it gives the abstract mathematical structure of events and says nothing about the intrinsic character of whatever has that structure. Feser draws the conclusion (step 11): because structure requires a bearer, physics itself implies there is more to reality than physics describes.

Two qualifications keep this from being misread. First, Feser is not saying physics is false or merely subjective; its description is accurate as far as it goes. Abstraction is legitimate as long as we remember we are doing it. Second, he is not arguing from what physics has *not yet* discovered. The limitation is one of principle, not of current progress, so no future physics could remove it without ceasing to be the mathematical discipline it is.

People often think that if physics “reduces” color to wavelengths, it has shown that color as we experience it is unreal. Feser’s reply is that the experienced quality was excluded from the description by stipulation, not by discovery. The method guaranteed it would be missing.

checks.q: In the airplane example, what is the WORSE of the two mistakes Feser describes?
options: Using averages instead of actual weights
Insisting that because the engineers’ data say nothing about meal preferences, there are no such preferences
Relying on engineers for weight calculations
Letting caterers see the engineers’ data
checks.explanation: Relying only on the data would be silly; concluding there is no fact of the matter about preferences mistakes the method’s silence for a discovery.

checks.q: Why does Feser think Russell’s point implies there is MORE to reality than physics describes?
options: Because Russell believed in God
Because physics contains errors
Because there can be no structure without something that has the structure, and physics gives only structure
Because physics cannot measure small enough quantities
checks.explanation: This is the move from step 10 to step 11: structure requires a bearer whose intrinsic nature physics leaves unspecified.

checks.q: Which statement best captures why the limitation Feser describes cannot be removed by future progress in physics?
options: It follows from physics’ method of describing only what can be modeled mathematically
Physics has already reached its final theory
Scientists lack funding
Future physics will abandon mathematics
checks.explanation: The limitation is one of principle: it comes from the quantitative method itself, not from current ignorance.

summary.plain: Physics describes the world using math, so it only notices what can be measured and put into equations. That’s why it’s so powerful — but it also means it leaves out things like colors as we see them, meanings, and purposes, not because they aren’t real but because it never looks for them. It’s like engineers who treat airline passengers as average weights: useful, but nobody concludes the passengers have no taste in food.

summary.heading: Problem 3: laws of nature cannot be the ultimate explanation
summary.body:
Science explains by appeal to laws, but any appeal to laws (or to Krauss’ proposed layers of laws) raises the questions of what a law is, how it has any power to do anything, and where it comes from — questions scientific explanation, which presupposes laws, cannot answer. Feser surveys the main philosophical theories of laws and argues that none helps scientism:

- **Aristotelian:** a law is shorthand for how a thing will behave given its nature or essence. Then laws presuppose the existence and activity of the things that follow them, so they cannot explain the existence of those things — and cannot explain the existence of the universe, contra Krauss.
- **Cartesian-Newtonian:** laws are a theological notion — God has set things up to behave in regular ways. Then God does the real explaining, which is no help to an atheist wielding scientism.
- **Humean:** laws merely summarize regularities we happen to observe. Then they tell us *that* a regularity exists, not *why* — they re-describe rather than explain.
- **Platonic:** laws are abstract objects in which physical things “participate.” Then we still need to know why there is a physical world participating in them, and in these laws rather than others — which requires something beyond the laws.

So these are questions only philosophy can answer, because they concern what every scientific explanation takes for granted. Nor can the scientism defender reply that ultimate explanation is unavailable anyway: that is itself a philosophical claim, and a false one, since it violates the principle of sufficient reason defended in chapter 5.
summary.takeaway: Whatever laws of nature are — descriptions of natures, divine decrees, regularities, or abstract objects — they presuppose something beyond themselves, so science’s appeal to laws cannot be the ultimate explanation of the world.
summary.deepDive:
The hardest idea here is that **laws presuppose what they govern**. It helps to picture how people often imagine laws: as invisible rules hovering over the universe, pushing things around. Feser’s survey of the four main philosophical theories shows that on none of them can a law do what that picture suggests — namely, explain why there is a world at all (steps 12–13).

Take a thought experiment. Imagine the law of gravitation holding in a universe that contains no masses whatsoever. What would it govern? Nothing. On the **Aristotelian** view, that is because a law is just a summary of how things with certain natures behave; no things, no behavior, no law. So the law cannot explain the existence of the things — which is exactly why Hawking and Mlodinow’s “because there is a law like gravity the universe can create itself” fails, a point Feser already pressed against Krauss in Part A.

On the **Cartesian-Newtonian** view, a law is shorthand for God’s decree that bodies behave regularly. Then it is God, not the law, who explains — hardly a help to atheism. On the **Humean** view, a law is merely a summary of observed regularity: A’s are regularly followed by B’s. Ask “why are A’s followed by B’s?” and the Humean law answers, in effect, “because A’s are regularly followed by B’s.” That is a redescription, not an explanation. On the **Platonic** view, laws are abstract objects that physical things “participate in.” But then we must still ask why there is a physical world participating in them, and in these laws rather than others — questions that point beyond the laws.

Notice the structure of Feser’s argument: it is a *dilemma with four horns*. He doesn’t need to decide which theory of laws is correct. Whichever you pick, laws cannot be ultimate. That is what secures step 13.

The fallback — “ultimate explanation just isn’t available, so science can’t be faulted” — fails twice (step 14). It is a philosophical claim, not a scientific result, so asserting it already concedes that science isn’t the only source of knowledge. And it contradicts the principle of sufficient reason, defended in chapter 5.

People often confuse *describing* how things behave with *explaining why anything exists to behave*. Physics does the first magnificently. The five proofs are concerned with the second, which is why no advance in physics could make them obsolete — and why the next objection, that the laws are simply a brute fact, is the atheist’s natural retreat.

checks.q: On the Aristotelian view of laws, why can laws not explain the existence of the universe?
options: Because laws are God’s decrees
Because laws are only summaries of regularities
Because laws exist in a Platonic realm
Because laws describe how existing things act given their natures, and so presuppose those things
checks.explanation: Aristotelian laws presuppose the things whose natures they describe, so they cannot account for those things’ existence.

checks.q: Why is Feser’s argument about laws effective even without deciding which theory of laws is true?
options: Because all four theories are false
Because Feser proves the Aristotelian theory first
Because on every one of the main theories, laws still fail to be the ultimate explanation
Because science has already decided the question
checks.explanation: The argument works like a multi-horned dilemma: whichever view you hold, something beyond the laws is required.

checks.q: What two problems does Feser find with the claim that “ultimate explanation is not to be had anyway”?
options: It is unscientific and unpopular
It is a philosophical rather than scientific claim, and it violates the principle of sufficient reason
It contradicts quantum mechanics and relativity
It was refuted by Hume and by Kant
checks.explanation: Asserting it concedes that there is non-scientific knowledge, and PSR (chapter 5) shows it to be false.

summary.plain: Science explains things by pointing to “laws of nature.” But that raises new questions: what is a law, and why does it hold? Feser shows that whatever you think a law is, it can’t be the final explanation of why anything exists at all — it always depends on something else.

summary.heading: Problem 4: the argument from success is a non sequitur
summary.body:
Why do smart people accept scientism anyway? Borrowing a phrase from Wittgenstein, Feser says a picture holds them captive: the dazzling predictive and technological success of science. Rosenberg argues that the success of physics shows its methods are the right ones for acquiring *all* knowledge and that physics is the whole truth about reality. Many scientism advocates would widen this to include chemistry and biology, but they share the core inference, which Feser reduces to two steps: science’s predictive power and technology are unmatched by any rival source of knowledge; therefore what science reveals is probably all that is real.

That is as bad as arguing that because metal detectors find coins and metal objects better than any other method, metallic objects are probably all that exist. Metal detectors are tuned to one aspect of the world; even a perfect success rate would not make it likely that nothing else exists. Physics brilliantly captures the aspects of nature that can be modeled mathematically — it doesn’t follow that there are no other aspects.

Rosenberg adds that critics of scientism are inconsistent: they trust their cardiologist, mechanic, and software engineer, but cry “scientism” when their music, morals, or metaphysics are subjected to science. Feser replies that this is like saying you can’t trust metal detectors to detect anything unless you think they alone detect physical objects. To object that metal detectors cover part of reality while science covers the whole of it simply begs the question at issue.

The same fallacy appears whenever a scientism advocate demands a list of the predictive successes of metaphysics or theology and declares victory when none is offered — like demanding the metal-detecting achievements of gardening, cooking, and painting and concluding that spades, spatulas, and brushes should be replaced by metal detectors. A method that is very useful for the predictable and controllable aspects of the world does not show those aspects are all there is. Such thinkers resemble the drunk who searches only under the streetlamp because that is where the light is, and concludes the keys can be nowhere else.
summary.takeaway: Science’s unmatched success shows that its methods are reliable within their domain, not that its domain is all of reality — exactly as a metal detector’s success shows nothing about whether non-metallic things exist.
summary.deepDive:
The key to this section is seeing that the argument from success changes its subject between premise and conclusion. The premise is about *reliability*: science predicts and controls brilliantly. The conclusion is about *scope*: what science reveals is probably all that is real. Success is excellent evidence of reliability within a domain. It is no evidence at all that the domain has no outside (steps 15–16).

Feser grants Rosenberg more than people expect. He does not deny that the precision of physics would be “a miracle” if its methods were unreliable. He agrees that physics does what it does brilliantly. What he denies is the extra step from “reliable at what it does” to “what it does covers everything.” The metal detector makes the gap visible: even a detector that never once failed would leave the existence of wood, water, and people entirely open.

A worked example: consider a superb radiologist who reads X-rays with perfect accuracy. Her track record is excellent evidence that X-rays reveal bone fractures reliably. Would it be evidence that patients have no feelings, no memories, and no plans for the weekend, because X-rays never show them? Obviously not. X-rays are tuned to one kind of feature. So is mathematical physics.

Rosenberg’s inconsistency charge — you trust your cardiologist but cry “scientism” about your metaphysics — has the same structure. Trusting an instrument within its range does not commit you to believing it has no range limits. The only way to make the charge stick is to assume that science’s range is unlimited — which is the very conclusion in dispute. That is why Feser says the reply “metal detectors detect part of reality, science the whole” simply begs the question.

The same fallacy drives a common debating move: demanding a list of the predictions and technologies produced by metaphysics or theology, and declaring victory when none appears. Feser’s parody — demanding the metal-detecting achievements of gardening, cooking, and painting — shows the demand presupposes that prediction and control are the only marks of knowledge. And the drunk under the streetlamp shows the psychology: he searches where the light is and concludes the keys can be nowhere else.

People often think that rejecting this argument means doubting vaccines or airplanes. It doesn’t. You can trust every well-established scientific result and still deny that science is the only way to know anything. That is Feser’s position exactly, and it is what makes step 19 — no good argument for scientism — secure.

checks.q: What is the logical flaw in the argument from science’s success, as Feser presents it?
options: It moves from evidence of reliability within a domain to a conclusion about the domain being all of reality
It relies on false data about scientific predictions
It assumes physics is finished
It confuses biology with physics
checks.explanation: The premise concerns how well science works; the conclusion concerns how much reality there is. Success supports the first, not the second.

checks.q: Why does the reply “metal detectors detect only part of reality, but science detects the whole” fail?
options: Because metal detectors are also scientific instruments
Because science does not detect anything
Because it is too complicated
Because it simply assumes the point in dispute — that science covers the whole of reality
checks.explanation: Whether science describes the whole of reality is exactly the question at issue, so asserting it begs the question.

checks.q: Which image does Feser use to capture the psychology of the scientism advocate?
options: A child refusing to do homework
The drunk who searches for his keys only under the streetlamp
A thief demanding the police car’s papers
A shelf held up by brackets let go in midair
checks.explanation: The drunk searches where the light is and concludes the keys can be nowhere else — as scientism looks only where its method shines.

summary.plain: The main reason people believe science is the only source of knowledge is that it works so well. But working well at one job doesn’t mean it’s the only job. A metal detector is the best way to find coins, yet that doesn’t prove only metal exists.

summary.heading: Scientism’s fallback positions: “worth knowing” and “conceptual analysis”
summary.body:
A retreat: perhaps science can’t answer every question, but philosophy’s questions lack crisp, consensus answers and produce no technology, so science tells us everything *worth* knowing. Feser gives two replies. First, this is like taking only the classes you know you will ace and then citing your GPA as proof of your brilliance. If only the predictable, controllable, consensus-generating counts as “science,” science will trivially be one long success story — that says nothing about whether the questions it excludes matter. Second, the claim that only such questions are worth pursuing is itself a philosophical claim needing philosophical defense; once again, trying to avoid going beyond science requires going beyond it.

A more sophisticated move (Feser cites James Ladyman and Don Ross’s program of “naturalized” metaphysics): unless philosophy is just an extension of science, all it can be is **conceptual analysis**, which appeals to intuitions and folk notions that may not track reality — it tells us how we think, not how the world is. Feser calls this a false alternative, a variant of **Hume’s Fork** (all objects of inquiry are either relations of ideas or matters of fact). Hume’s Fork is notoriously self-refuting: it is neither a conceptual truth nor an empirically testable fact. The modern version — every legitimate inquiry is either conceptual analysis or natural science — likewise is neither, and no evidence from natural science could support it. (In a footnote he adds that appealing to neuroscience or cognitive science here would beg the question, since whether those sciences are our only source of knowledge about cognition is exactly what is disputed.) The scientism advocate takes up a third cognitive stance toward reality in the very act of denying that one exists.

Moreover, the truths of **logic and mathematics** fit neither tine: they have a necessity natural science lacks and an objectivity mere conceptual analysis cannot guarantee. Attempts to deny their necessity or objectivity face notorious difficulties (see chapter 3), and the only motive for them is to save scientism. The truths of natural theology, Feser argues, are like these: necessary and objective yet neither empirical-scientific nor merely conceptual. If the scientism advocate cannot see how such knowledge is possible, that is his problem: he already possesses oceans of knowledge he cannot account for — logic, mathematics, and his own fork. He is like a thief caught with the loot who demands that the arresting officers produce the ownership papers for their squad car.
summary.takeaway: The retreats to “science covers everything worth knowing” and “anything else is mere conceptual analysis” are themselves non-scientific claims that refute themselves — and logic and mathematics, like natural theology, fit neither of scientism’s two boxes.
summary.deepDive:
The most instructive thing to do with **Hume’s Fork** is to apply it to itself, slowly. The Fork says every legitimate object of inquiry is either a relation of ideas (true by the meanings of terms, like “all bachelors are unmarried”) or a matter of fact (known by observation, like “water boils at 100°C at sea level”). Now ask: which kind of claim is the Fork itself? Is it true by definition? No — you can deny it without contradicting yourself, as generations of philosophers have. Is it a matter of fact established by observation? No — no experiment could reveal that all knowledge divides into two kinds. So by its own standard, the Fork is neither, and should be consigned to the flames Hume reserved for such claims. It refutes itself. Ladyman and Ross’s modern version — every legitimate inquiry is either natural science or conceptual analysis — fails the same test (step 18).

Feser draws a striking conclusion: in the very act of denying that there is a third kind of cognitive stance toward reality, the scientism advocate occupies one. And he adds a footnote worth remembering: appealing to neuroscience or cognitive science to support the dichotomy would beg the question, since whether those sciences are our only source of knowledge about the mind is exactly what is disputed.

Logic and mathematics make the point concrete. That 7 + 5 = 12 is **necessary**: it could not have been otherwise, unlike the boiling point of water, which depends on how nature happens to be. And it is **objective**: it would be true even if no one had ever formed the relevant concepts, so it is not merely a fact about our ideas. So such truths are neither empirical findings nor mere conceptual mapping. Chapter 3 defended their necessity and objectivity; Feser notes that the only motive for denying them is to save scientism.

The truths of natural theology, Feser argues, belong in the same third category — necessary, objective, known by reason from premises every science presupposes. The thief-and-squad-car image makes the dialectical point: someone who relies daily on knowledge he cannot account for (logic, mathematics, his own Fork) is in no position to demand that the natural theologian produce credentials.

The “worth knowing” retreat (step 17) fails more simply. The GPA analogy shows that defining success by what your method can already handle guarantees success trivially. And the claim that only such questions matter is a value judgment about inquiry — philosophy again. People often think “non-empirical” means “made up”; logic and mathematics show that some of our most certain knowledge is non-empirical.

checks.q: Why is Hume’s Fork self-refuting?
options: Because Hume later abandoned it
Because it is neither true by definition nor established by observation, so by its own standard it is not knowledge
Because it is contradicted by quantum physics
Because it applies only to mathematics
checks.explanation: Applied to itself, the Fork fits neither of its two categories.

checks.q: Truths of logic and mathematics fall between the tines of the fork because they are…
options: probable and useful
empirical and revisable
necessary (unlike scientific findings) and objective (unlike mere conceptual analysis)
known only by revelation
checks.explanation: Their necessity sets them apart from empirical science; their objectivity sets them apart from mere concept-mapping.

checks.q: A critic says, “Of course science succeeds — it only tackles questions that can be answered with consensus, and those are the only ones worth asking.” Which analogy fits Feser’s reply?
options: The thief and the squad car
The airplane engineers
The metal detector
The student who takes only easy classes and cites his GPA
checks.explanation: Restricting yourself to what you’re sure to ace guarantees a great record but shows nothing about the worth of what you avoided.

summary.plain: Some people back off and say science at least covers everything worth knowing, or that any other kind of thinking is just playing with words. Feser shows both claims can’t pass their own tests. Math and logic are real knowledge that isn’t science and isn’t mere word-play — and he argues knowledge of God is like that too.

summary.heading: Objection: the fundamental laws are just a brute fact
summary.body:
Suppose the atheist concedes everything so far — Hume and quantum mechanics haven’t undermined the principle that everything has an explanation, science can’t explain its own fundamental laws, and philosophy is a real source of explanation. He might still say the fundamental laws simply *have* no explanation of any kind; everything else is explained by them, but they are just there. Feser notes that Mackie and Russell essentially held this.

Three problems:

1. It contradicts the **principle of sufficient reason**, which chapter 5 argued is true. So it is a nonstarter.
2. It is **ad hoc**: there is no motive for it except avoiding arguments like those in the book — ironic, since atheists often accuse theists of rigging premises to reach a desired conclusion. An independent motive would exist if the Humean or quantum-mechanical objections to PSR worked, but they don’t. And, as Lloyd Gerson observed (discussed in Part A), you cannot answer an argument that *offers* an explanation by saying “maybe there’s no explanation”; you must show what is wrong with the one given.
3. If the fundamental laws are unexplained, **no higher-level law explains anything** either. Explaining phenomenon P by law A, law A by law B, and then declaring B a brute fact is like setting a book on a shelf, the shelf on brackets, and then letting go of the brackets in midair and expecting everything to stay up. A regress of laws is like a hierarchical causal series (chapter 1): it must end in something self-explanatory that can impart explanatory power without borrowing it. Neither the unexplained nor the explained-by-another can do that; only what is purely actual, without parts, whose essence is existence, and so absolutely necessary.
summary.takeaway: Treating the fundamental laws as a brute fact contradicts PSR, is motivated only by avoiding the proofs, and would leave every law resting on it without real explanatory power — a regress of explanations must end in something self-explanatory.
summary.deepDive:
This objection is the natural retreat after the previous section: “All right, science can’t explain its deepest laws — so nothing does. They’re just there.” Feser’s third reply is the one to understand deeply, and a thought experiment helps.

Imagine borrowing money. You borrow ten dollars from Ann; Ann borrowed it from Bob; Bob from Carla; and so on. If every person in the chain merely borrowed, the question “where did the money come from?” is never answered, however long the chain. At some point there must be someone who actually *has* money that isn’t borrowed. Explanatory power works the same way. When law A explains an event, it does so only because law B explains A, and so on. If the last law explains nothing — if it is a brute fact — then the explanatory power that was supposedly flowing down the chain never had a source. Feser’s image is a book on a shelf, the shelf on brackets, and the brackets let go in midair. This is the hierarchical (per se) series of chapter 1 in explanatory form (step 21).

What can end such a regress? Not something unexplained (it has no explanatory power to give), and not something explained by another (it just adds a link to the chain). Only something **self-explanatory**, which can impart explanatory power without deriving it: in Feser’s terms, something purely actual, without parts, whose essence is existence, and therefore absolutely necessary.

This answers a common confusion. People often say, “Theists also stop somewhere — at God — so God is their brute fact.” But the question was never *whether* explanation stops; it is *where* and *why*. A contingent law, which could have been otherwise, cries out for explanation. A being whose very nature is to exist does not; its existence is explained by what it is. The theist’s stopping point is self-explanatory, not brute.

The first two replies deserve mention too. The brute-fact view contradicts PSR (chapter 5). And it is ad hoc: there is no independent motivation for it now that the Humean and quantum-mechanical objections to PSR have failed (Part A), which Feser notes is ironic, since atheists often accuse theists of rigging premises. Finally, Lloyd Gerson’s point: when someone has *offered* an explanation, you cannot dismiss it by saying “maybe there is no explanation.” You have to show what is wrong with the explanation on the table. Mackie and Russell, whom Feser names here, never did that for arguments like the five proofs.

checks.q: What is the point of Feser’s image of a book on a shelf held by brackets that are let go in midair?
options: Physical laws are like furniture
If the deepest law is unexplained, the laws depending on it don’t really explain anything either
The universe is unstable
Explanations should be short
checks.explanation: Borrowed explanatory power needs a source; a brute-fact foundation supplies none.

checks.q: Why is the theist’s stopping point not simply another brute fact, according to Feser?
options: Because theists refuse to answer the question
Because God is very powerful
Because God is self-explanatory — purely actual, simple, his essence identical to existence, and necessary
Because God is more popular than the laws of physics
checks.explanation: The regress must end in something that explains itself; a contingent law cannot, but a being whose essence is existence can.

checks.q: Which of the following is one of Feser’s three problems with the brute-fact view?
options: It was never held by any serious philosopher
It contradicts the second law of thermodynamics
It makes science impossible to teach
It contradicts the principle of sufficient reason
checks.explanation: The three problems: it contradicts PSR, it is ad hoc, and it drains higher-level laws of explanatory power.

summary.plain: Some say the deepest laws of physics are simply there, with no explanation. Feser says that if the bottom layer explains nothing, then nothing built on it is really explained either — like a shelf whose supports are floating in midair. The chain of explanations has to end in something that explains itself.

summary.heading: Objection: a designer would be more complex than the universe
summary.body:
This objection, going back to Hume and pressed by Dawkins, says any designer of the universe would be even more complex than the universe and so would itself need a cause. Feser says it should be obvious by now what is wrong.

It targets **design arguments** of the Paley or Intelligent Design type: natural objects like the eye or bacterial flagellum have many parts arranged just so, like human artifacts, which have intelligent designers; so by analogy, probably the natural objects do too. The critic replies that a designer like us would be complex in the same way and need its own explanation, so a more parsimonious explanation is likely correct.

The five proofs are nothing like this:

- **No appeal to complexity** in that sense. The Neo-Platonic proof does start from things having parts, but it doesn’t care how many, whether they must be arranged precisely, or whether they resemble artifacts. A pebble or a drop of water — which Paley would never cite — works as well as an eye.
- **No appeal to probability.** The proofs concern hierarchical causal series operating here and now, not linear series stretching back to the origin of species. And they are attempted strict demonstrations, not inductive or abductive inferences, so it misses the point to propose that some rival explanation is more probable or parsimonious. To refute them you must show a premise is false, the conclusion doesn’t follow, or the argument begs the question.
- **Most importantly**, the proofs *agree* that a complex cause would need a cause. That is exactly why they conclude that the ultimate cause is absolutely simple, without parts. That is true of the God they reach and of no terminus the atheist proposes. As an objection to this kind of natural theology, it completely misses the point.
summary.takeaway: The complex-designer objection targets probabilistic design arguments; the five proofs don’t rely on complexity or probability and actually agree that complex causes need causes — which is why they conclude to an absolutely simple first cause.
summary.deepDive:
The heart of this section is distinguishing two things that sound alike: **complexity** and **composition**. Complexity, in Paley’s sense, means having many parts arranged just so, in a way that serves a function — the eye, the bacterial flagellum, a watch. Composition means simply having parts of *any* kind: physical parts, or metaphysical ones like a distinction between a thing’s essence and its existence, or between its actuality and its potentiality. A pebble is not complex in Paley’s sense, but it is composite. The Neo-Platonic proof starts from composition, so a pebble or a drop of water is as good a starting point as an eye. No design theorist would ever pick a pebble. That alone shows the proofs are not design arguments.

Second, **probability**. A design argument says: given these intricate structures, a designer is the most probable explanation. That invites the reply that a naturalistic explanation might be more probable or parsimonious, especially if the designer is itself complex. But the five proofs are attempted strict demonstrations: they claim the conclusion follows with necessity from premises that are certain. They also concern hierarchical causes operating here and now, not a linear chain back to the origins of species. So “a simpler explanation is likelier” simply doesn’t engage them; to refute a demonstration you must show a false premise, an invalid inference, or a begged question (step 20).

Third — Feser’s “most importantly” — the proofs *agree* with Hume and Dawkins. Try it: take the objection’s own principle, “anything complex needs a cause beyond itself,” and apply it consistently. You cannot stop at anything with parts. You are driven to a cause with no parts at all. That is exactly the route the proofs take, and it is why they conclude to an absolutely simple God. Far from being refuted by the principle, the proofs are powered by it. By contrast, nothing an atheist offers as the terminus of explanation — the laws, the Big Bang, the multiverse — is simple in this sense.

People often think every argument for God is a version of Paley’s watchmaker. That confusion is what makes the objection seem devastating. Feser’s reply is not that design arguments are worthless (he doesn’t evaluate them here), but that his arguments are a different kind of thing, judged by different standards. This is a clear case of the “caricature” pattern in step 22.

A useful exercise: ask someone raising the objection whether the first cause they are criticizing has parts. If they say yes, point out that the proofs deny that; if they say no, the objection no longer applies.

checks.q: Why can a pebble serve as the starting point of the Neo-Platonic proof but not of Paley’s argument?
options: Because pebbles are designed
Because the Neo-Platonic proof needs only composition (having parts), not functional complexity
Because Paley disliked geology
Because pebbles are more probable than eyes
checks.explanation: Composition is enough for the Neo-Platonic proof; Paley needs intricate, function-serving arrangement.

checks.q: What does Feser call the most important reply to the complex-designer objection?
options: That Dawkins misunderstands evolution
That probabilistic arguments are always weak
That the proofs agree a complex cause would need a cause and therefore conclude to an absolutely simple one
That God is too mysterious to discuss
checks.explanation: The objection’s principle is one the proofs accept; it is what drives them to a noncomposite first cause.

checks.q: Someone says, “A naturalistic explanation is more parsimonious than God.” Why does Feser think this misses the five proofs?
options: Because the proofs are strict demonstrations, not hypotheses to be weighed by parsimony or probability
Because parsimony favors God
Because naturalistic explanations are always complex
Because Ockham was a theist
checks.explanation: Parsimony is a criterion for choosing among rival hypotheses; a demonstration is refuted only by showing a false premise or invalid step.

terms: The five proofs (Aristotelian, Neo-Platonic, Augustinian, Thomistic, rationalist)
summary.plain: A famous objection says: if a designer made the universe, the designer must be even more complicated and would need its own designer. Feser replies that his arguments aren’t about complicated designs at all — and they agree that anything made of parts needs a cause, which is why they conclude that God has no parts.

summary.heading: Objection: go “one god further”
summary.body:
Dawkins (in a lecture) and Colin McGinn (in print) argue that monotheists already reject Zeus, Venus, Thor, Quetzalcoatl and the rest, so to be consistent they should reject one more god. First reply: there are at least five demonstrations of the God of Western monotheism and no one claims arguments for Zeus. There is no inconsistency in affirming the one and denying the others, and anyone who says otherwise must answer the arguments rather than glibly lump God in with the pagan pantheon.

The deeper problem is that the objection misunderstands what the debate between atheism and classical theism (Aristotle, Plotinus, Augustine, Maimonides, Avicenna, Aquinas, Leibniz) is about. It pictures God as one more member of a class of unusual “supernatural beings,” like werewolves or ghosts. But the God of classical theism is:

- not a member of any genus or species, including “gods,” since that would make him composite (genus plus difference), and he is simple;
- not sharing an essence with other “gods,” since that would mean a distinction of essence and existence in him, whereas he is existence itself;
- not one cause among many but the purely actual actualizer, the source of the causal power of everything else — including Zeus and company, were they real.

The pagan gods of the stories are limited: fluctuating emotions, bodies, beginnings, parents, frustrated plans, ignorance, vices. The God of classical theism is immutable, immaterial, eternal, uncaused, omnipotent, omniscient, perfectly good. Each pagan god is *a being* among beings; God is not “a being” that has and derives existence but subsistent being itself, from which all else derives.

Feser’s analogies: imagine an anti-Euclidean who says, “You agree that every drawn triangle has imperfectly straight sides; I just go one step further and say triangularity itself has imperfectly straight sides.” Or an anti-Platonist: “You agree every good thing is imperfectly good; I just extend that to the Form of the Good.” These are category mistakes — treating the standard as one more instance measured by it. The point holds *whether or not* Euclid or Plato is right: if space is non-Euclidean, Euclidean triangles are simply uninstantiated, not imperfectly straight; if the Third Man argument works, there is no Form of the Good, not an imperfect one. Likewise, even if atheism were true, it would not be because God turned out to be one more nonexistent member of the class of gods. That suggestion does not even make sense.
summary.takeaway: “One god further” is a category mistake: the God of classical theism is not one member of the class “gods” but being itself, so rejecting him is not a larger dose of the same disbelief that rejects Zeus.
summary.deepDive:
To see why this is a category mistake rather than a clever point, you need to understand *why* classical theism says God is not a member of any kind.

Start with how kinds work. A dog is an animal (the **genus**) of a particular sort (the **specific difference** — canine). Belonging to a kind means being a combination: the general nature plus what distinguishes you within it. If God were one of the “gods,” he would be a combination of godhood-in-general plus what makes him this god rather than that one — and so he would be composite. But the proofs conclude that the first cause is absolutely simple (chapter 2, chapter 6). So he cannot belong to any genus, “gods” included.

Next, sharing an essence. Zeus and Thor, if real, would share a nature (being a god) while each having his own existence — the nature is one thing, the fact that this instance of it exists is another. That is the essence/existence distinction of the Thomistic proof. God, the proofs argue, is the one being in whom there is no such distinction: his essence just *is* to exist. So he cannot share a nature with anything.

Third, causation. Zeus in the myths is one cause among others — he throws thunderbolts, but so do storms. God, as purely actual actualizer, is the source of the causal power of *everything*, which would include Zeus if Zeus existed.

Feser’s analogies make the logical shape vivid. An anti-Euclidean who says, “You deny drawn triangles are perfectly straight; I just go one step further to triangularity itself,” has not extended a doubt; he has confused the standard with one of its instances. And here is the subtle point Feser insists on: this is so *whether or not* Euclid is right. If space turned out non-Euclidean, the result would not be that Euclidean triangles have crooked sides — that makes no sense — but that there are no Euclidean triangles in physical space. Likewise, if atheism were true, it would not be because God turned out to be one more nonexistent god. The objection misdescribes what the atheist would even be claiming.

A course illustration: disbelieving in Hamlet and disbelieving in Shakespeare are different kinds of claim, supported by entirely different evidence. (Like all analogies for God it limps; God is not a being alongside the world as an author is alongside his play.)

People often suspect this is a redefinition invented to dodge the objection. It isn’t: Feser lists Aristotle, Plotinus, Augustine, Maimonides, Avicenna, Aquinas, and Leibniz — the classical conception long predates the objection. And Feser’s first reply still stands alongside it: there are arguments for God and none for Zeus (step 22).

checks.q: Why, according to classical theism, can God not be a member of the genus “gods”?
options: Because belonging to a genus would make him composite (general nature plus distinguishing difference), and he is simple
Because there are too many gods to count
Because the genus “gods” is fictional
Because God is younger than the pagan gods
checks.explanation: Membership in a kind means being a combination of genus and difference; divine simplicity rules that out.

checks.q: What is Feser’s FIRST, simpler reply to the “one god further” objection?
options: God is not a being
Zeus had parents
There are at least five demonstrations of the God of classical theism and no arguments for Zeus, so there is no inconsistency
Monotheism is older than polytheism
checks.explanation: The deeper reply (category mistake) comes second; the first is the difference in evidence.

checks.q: If physical space turned out to be non-Euclidean, what would follow for Feser’s anti-Euclidean analogy?
options: Euclidean triangles would have crooked sides
Triangularity would be refuted as incoherent
Euclid would be shown to be an atheist
Euclidean triangles would simply have no physical instances — which shows the anti-Euclidean’s claim was confused either way
checks.explanation: The point about category mistakes holds whether or not the view in question is true.

summary.plain: “You don’t believe in Zeus or Thor — just go one god further.” Feser says this treats God as one more superhero-like being in the world. But the God of the proofs isn’t one more thing that exists; he’s the source of existence itself — a completely different kind of claim.

summary.heading: Objection: the philosophers’ God is not the God of ordinary believers
summary.body:
Some critics grant, for the sake of argument, that the proofs might establish a purely actual, absolutely simple First Cause — and then add that such an abstraction is not the God that ordinary people pray to, read about in scripture, and worship. So even a successful proof would leave religion as actually practiced unsupported. Feser finds two problems with this objection.

First, it would be **irrelevant** even if it were true. If the arguments succeed, the God of philosophical theism exists, and therefore atheism is false. That is the whole point of the book. What would remain open is a different question: whether some religion — Judaism, Christianity, Islam, or another — gives further, divinely revealed knowledge about this God. That is a serious debate, but it is a debate among theists, not between theism and atheism. (Feser made the same point in the book’s introduction.)

Second, it is **false**. Some religions explicitly identify the God of the philosophers with the God of worship. Standard Catholic teaching holds that the God of the Bible and the God knowable by philosophical argument are one and the same. Some things about him — for instance, that he is omnipotent and omniscient — can be known both through philosophical argument and through revelation; others, such as that he is a Trinity, can be known only through revelation. But it is one God known by different routes, and other religions make comparable claims.

What about the ordinary person in the pew, who has never heard of divine simplicity, the essence/existence distinction, or act and potency? Feser’s analogy is the layman and the atom. Many people picture molecules as little balls connected by sticks. That picture is crude, yet they really do believe in atoms and molecules — the same ones physicists study — just with a less sophisticated understanding. Likewise, the ordinary believer holds that God caused the world, is unique, is uncaused and never came into existence, and is all-powerful, all-knowing, and all-good. He cannot articulate or defend these beliefs as a philosopher would, but it is the same God, less technically understood.
summary.takeaway: If the proofs work, atheism is false regardless — and the God of the philosophers is the same God ordinary believers worship, known through a different route and understood with less technical precision.
summary.deepDive:
The hardest idea here is how two people with very different conceptions can be thinking about the **same thing**. Philosophers call this the difference between how something is presented to you and what it is you are talking about. A classic example (a course illustration, from the philosopher Frege): ancient observers called a bright object in the morning sky the Morning Star and a bright object in the evening sky the Evening Star. They had very different descriptions in mind, yet both names referred to one thing — the planet Venus. Discovering that fact was a discovery about one object, not the replacement of two objects by a third.

Feser’s own analogy is similar. The layman’s ball-and-stick picture of a molecule is far cruder than the physicist’s equations, and even partly wrong. But when the layman says “water is made of molecules,” he is talking about the very molecules the physicist studies. A crude grasp of something is still a grasp of *that* thing. The ordinary believer’s beliefs — God is the uncaused, unique, eternal, all-powerful, all-knowing, all-good cause of the world — pick out the same being the proofs arrive at. The philosopher’s account adds precision and defense, not a different God.

The Catholic teaching Feser cites fits this model neatly. Reason and revelation are two routes to one God. Some truths are reachable by both (omnipotence, omniscience); some only by revelation (the Trinity). Just as you could learn that Venus is a planet either by telescope or by testimony, while some facts about it might be learnable only one way.

Why does Feser also call the objection irrelevant? Because of what the book is trying to establish. Its target is atheism. If any version of the proofs succeeds, there is a purely actual, simple, necessary cause of all things — and atheism is false whatever further details are true. The objection concedes the book’s main conclusion and changes the subject to comparative religion.

People often cite Pascal’s contrast between “the God of Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob” and “the God of the philosophers” as if it meant two different beings. A charitable reading is that Pascal contrasts two ways of *knowing* God — as a living presence versus as the conclusion of an argument — which is compatible with Feser’s view that it is one God. This is a course note; Feser does not discuss Pascal here.

In conversation, this reply is often reassuring to believers who fear that philosophy replaces faith: it doesn’t; it shows by reason something about the God they already worship.

checks.q: Why does Feser say the objection would be irrelevant even if true?
options: Because philosophy and religion never overlap
Because if the proofs succeed, atheism is false, and what remains is a debate among theists about revelation
Because most people are not religious
Because the Bible does not mention God’s attributes
checks.explanation: The book’s target is atheism; the objection concedes the main conclusion and shifts to a debate among theists.

checks.q: According to the Catholic teaching Feser cites, which truth about God is knowable ONLY by revelation?
options: That God is a Trinity
That God is omnipotent
That God is omniscient
That God caused the world
checks.explanation: Omnipotence and omniscience can be known both by reason and revelation; the Trinity only by revelation.

checks.q: What does the ball-and-stick molecule analogy show?
options: That ordinary believers are irrational
That science is simpler than theology
That a crude, partly mistaken understanding of something can still be a belief in that very thing
That philosophers should use models
checks.explanation: The layman believes in the same atoms physicists study, just less sophisticatedly — as the ordinary believer does in the same God.

summary.plain: Some say the “God of philosophy” isn’t the God people pray to. Feser answers that if the proofs work, atheism is false anyway. And it’s the same God: ordinary believers just understand him less technically, the way most people picture atoms as little balls but still believe in the same atoms scientists study.

summary.heading: The problem of evil (I): defense versus theodicy, and Mackie’s logical argument
summary.body:
Philosophers distinguish two questions: is evil logically consistent with God’s existence, and if so, why does God permit it? Answering the first is a **defense**; answering the second is a **theodicy**. (Feser notes older Thomistic works used “theodicy” as a synonym for natural theology in general.) One can show compatibility without claiming to know God’s specific reasons, and a defense suffices to rebut the objection, so that is Feser’s focus.

J. L. Mackie’s logical argument: God is supposedly omnipotent and wholly good; an omnipotent being faces no limits, and a good being eliminates evil as far as it can; so God would be able and willing to eliminate all evil; yet evil exists. Feser says chapter 6’s treatment of omnipotence and goodness shows the problem lies in the second premise, which fails twice:

- Omnipotence has limits of a kind: even God can’t make a round square or make 2 + 2 = 5, because contradictions aren’t things to be done. If some goods logically cannot be had without permitting certain evils, God can’t have the goods without the evils.
- A good being does *not* necessarily eliminate every evil it can, because doing so might eliminate goods that presuppose those evils. A good parent could remove the misery of homework by cancelling it, but won’t, since that would sacrifice the child’s learning and obedience.

The classic example is free will: it is good that there be free creatures rather than automata, but free creatures can do evil. Mackie replied that God could have made free creatures who always freely choose good. Some theists (Plantinga is the best known) deny that God could guarantee this, but Feser says the theist need not take that route. Grant Mackie that God could create a world with free will, no evil, and even morally significant choices (not murdering, not stealing). Such a world still could not contain *all the moral goods of this one*. Forgiveness and mercy require real wrongdoing; courage requires danger; compassion requires misfortune; sacrifice requires giving up something good (compare John Hick’s “soul-making” theme). So what matters is not free will in the abstract but the virtues only a world containing evil makes possible. Mackie’s argument fails — as Mackie himself later conceded.

A footnote adds that this is not Leibniz’s claim that ours is the best possible world or that God must create the best: God could have created nothing, or a world better in various respects. Having made this world, God permits its evils because he draws from them goods not otherwise possible.
summary.takeaway: Evil does not contradict God’s existence, because omnipotence does not include contradictions and some real goods — forgiveness, mercy, courage, compassion, sacrifice — logically require the existence of evil.
summary.deepDive:
Begin with the logical shape of Mackie’s argument, because Feser’s reply is surgical. The argument has three claims that are supposed to be jointly inconsistent: (a) God is omnipotent, (b) God is perfectly good, (c) evil exists. To get a contradiction, Mackie needs a bridge premise: an omnipotent being can do anything, and a good being eliminates evil as far as it can. Feser targets only this bridge.

First clause: *omnipotence has no limits*. On the classical understanding (chapter 6), omnipotence is the power to do whatever is intrinsically possible. A round square is not a task God is too weak for; it is not a task at all — the words describe nothing. So if there are goods that logically cannot exist unless some evil exists, then not even God can have those goods without that evil.

Second clause: *a good being eliminates evil as far as it can*. Feser’s homework case refutes this. A parent *can* eliminate the misery of homework by cancelling it. A good parent won’t, because the misery is bound up with goods — learning, respect for reasonable authority. So a good being may permit an evil it could prevent, for the sake of a good that depends on it.

Now the crucial move, where Feser differs from many theists. Mackie says God could have made free creatures who always freely choose good. Plantinga famously denies God could guarantee this. Feser *grants* it — even with morally significant choices. His point is that such a world, though it contains free will, cannot contain certain goods that exist in ours. Work through them: **forgiveness** requires someone who actually did wrong; **mercy** requires a deserved punishment one refrains from inflicting; **courage** requires real danger; **compassion** requires real suffering; **sacrifice** requires really losing something good. These are goods that logically presuppose evil. That is why it is not free will in the abstract but these specific virtues that matter.

Two nuances. First, Feser’s footnote: this is not Leibniz’s claim that ours is the best possible world. God could have created nothing, or a world better in various respects. Given that he created this one, he permits its evils because he draws goods from them that would otherwise be impossible. Second, Feser offers a **defense**, not a **theodicy** — he shows compatibility without claiming to know God’s reason for any particular evil.

People often think the problem of evil is a knockdown refutation. Mackie himself later conceded that it does not show theism to be inconsistent. In terms of the module’s argument, this is one of the “wrong standard” objections of step 22: it assumes a conception of power and goodness that classical theism rejects.

checks.q: Which premise of Mackie’s argument does Feser target?
options: That evil exists
That God is perfectly good
The bridge premise that an omnipotent being has no limits and a good being eliminates all the evil it can
That God exists
checks.explanation: Feser locates the problem in Mackie’s second premise, with both of its clauses.

checks.q: Which good does Feser say logically requires that someone has ACTUALLY done evil?
options: Free will
Forgiveness
Knowledge
Physical health
checks.explanation: You cannot forgive where no wrong has been done. Free will itself does not require actual evil, as Feser grants Mackie.

checks.q: How does Feser’s reply differ from Plantinga’s?
options: Feser denies free will exists
Feser claims this is the best possible world
Feser argues God is not omnipotent
Feser grants that God could create free creatures who never sin, but argues such a world could not contain goods like forgiveness and courage
checks.explanation: Feser concedes Mackie’s point and relocates the issue to specific goods that require evil.

summary.plain: Does suffering prove there’s no God? Feser argues it doesn’t, because some of the best things in life — forgiving someone, being brave, showing compassion — can only exist where there is wrongdoing, danger, or pain. He doesn’t claim to know why any particular bad thing happens; he only shows that evil and a good God aren’t contradictory.

summary.heading: The problem of evil (II): Rowe’s evidential argument and the afterlife
summary.body:
The later Mackie and others shifted to an **evidential argument**: evil doesn’t disprove God, but it makes his nonexistence probable. William Rowe’s influential version: a perfect being would prevent any suffering it could prevent without losing a greater good or permitting an equal or worse evil; probably some actual suffering is like that; so probably there is no such being. His example: a fawn trapped in a forest fire caused by lightning, burned, and suffering for days before dying — suffering that seems pointless, redeemed by no virtue-building. Rowe concedes we cannot prove or know with certainty that no greater good comes from it; he claims only that it is rational to believe none does.

Feser’s reply: that belief is rational only if we lack independent reason to think God exists — and thus independent reason to think there *must* be a greater good even where we can’t see it. We have such reasons: five demonstrations of God and further arguments that he is omnipotent, omniscient, and perfectly good. Since Rowe admits a hidden greater good is possible, he must admit that independent proof of God gives reason to think such a good is actual. So the evidential argument poses no challenge to the book’s arguments; to challenge them it would first have to refute them independently — and if it could, it wouldn’t be needed.
