Feser adds that our ignorance of God’s reasons is exactly what we should expect, though fully showing this requires arguments beyond the book’s scope — especially for the immortality of the soul. Suppose there is an afterlife. Then this life’s evils could be unredeemable only if no good in the afterlife could outweigh them, which is absurd to claim: the afterlife would be endless while even the worst earthly sufferings end, and we are no more able to grasp it than a small child can grasp adulthood. Children often can’t see the point of homework, spinach, chores, or punishment until they grow up. God knows infinitely more than any parent, and the afterlife differs from this life far more than adulthood differs from childhood — so we should expect both that God can bring about an outweighing good and that we cannot yet see how. Developing this would be a theodicy; for a defense it is enough that such an afterlife is *possible*. Other aspects of evil (evil as privation; whether God must create the best world) were treated in chapter 6.
summary.takeaway: Rowe’s inference from “I can’t see a greater good” to “there probably is none” holds only if we lack independent evidence for a good God — and the proofs supply that evidence, while an afterlife makes our ignorance exactly what we should expect.
summary.deepDive:
Rowe’s argument is more modest than Mackie’s and so harder to dismiss. It doesn’t claim contradiction; it claims probability. So the key is to understand what makes a probability judgment rational: it must take into account *all* the relevant evidence, not just the evidence in front of you.

Worked example: you watch a surgeon make a deep incision in a patient. Taken by itself, cutting someone open looks like harm. If you knew nothing else, you might reasonably conclude the surgeon was cruel. But if you have strong independent evidence that the surgeon is skilled and benevolent — her record, her training, the hospital’s oversight — then it is rational to conclude that the incision serves a purpose, even if you have no idea what the purpose is. The same observation supports opposite conclusions depending on your other evidence.

Philosophers sometimes call this a **Moorean shift** (a course term, after G. E. Moore): if you have stronger reason to reject an argument’s conclusion than to accept one of its premises, you may reasonably run the argument backward. Rowe argues: if there is gratuitous suffering, there is no God; there is gratuitous suffering; so no God. Feser effectively argues: God exists (by independent demonstration); if God exists, there is no gratuitous suffering; so the fawn’s suffering is not gratuitous. Rowe himself concedes that a hidden greater good is *possible* and that we cannot know with certainty there is none — so he must admit that independent proof of God makes such a good actual.

This is why Feser says the evidential argument poses no challenge to the proofs: to challenge them it would first have to refute them, and if it could do that it would be unnecessary.

The afterlife point adds that our ignorance is *predictable*. If there is an endless life to come (Feser argues for the soul’s immortality elsewhere), then two things follow. Any finite suffering could be outweighed by an endless good. And we should no more expect to grasp that good now than a small child can grasp why homework, spinach, and discipline mattered until adulthood — with the gap between this life and the next far greater. For a *defense*, the mere possibility of such an afterlife is enough.

People often think Feser is claiming that the fawn will be compensated in heaven. He makes no such claim; animal suffering is not discussed in detail. His core reply does not depend on it: given independent proof of a good God, some greater good is served whether or not we can identify it. When talking with someone in pain, remember this is an answer to an argument, not a consolation to recite.

checks.q: What does Rowe himself concede about the fawn’s suffering?
options: That God exists
That we cannot prove or know with certainty that no greater good comes from it
That animals do not suffer
That the fawn goes to heaven
checks.explanation: Rowe claims only that it is rational to believe there is no greater good; he admits one is possible.

checks.q: What is the core of Feser’s reply to Rowe?
options: Belief that there is no greater good is rational only if we lack independent reason to think a good God exists — and the proofs provide such reason
The fawn story is fictional
Suffering is always a punishment for sin
Probability arguments are always invalid
checks.explanation: Independent evidence for a good God changes what is rational to believe about unseen goods.

checks.q: A friend says, “I can’t think of any good that justifies childhood cancer, so there probably isn’t one.” Which consideration from Feser most directly bears on the inference?
options: Cancer is caused by free will
Children are responsible for their illness
Feser’s list of virtues proves the good is courage
If there is independent proof of a good God, not seeing the reason is what we should expect, not evidence there is none
checks.explanation: Feser does not claim to identify the specific good; he challenges the step from “I can’t see one” to “there is none.” In real conversation, lead with compassion.

summary.plain: A more modest version says some suffering looks completely pointless, so God probably doesn’t exist. Feser replies that if we have good independent reasons to think God exists and is good, then “I can’t see the reason” doesn’t mean “there is no reason.” And if there’s a life after this one, it’s no surprise we can’t yet see how things will be made right.

summary.heading: Objection: divine hiddenness
summary.body:
The hiddenness argument (associated with J. L. Schellenberg) rests on two assumptions: if God existed, his existence would be obvious to most people; and it is not. Feser questions both.

**First assumption.** Schellenberg grounds it in the claim that God would want an explicit personal relationship with us, which presupposes our believing he exists. But not all theists think God intends that — Aristotle’s Unmoved Mover contemplates itself and takes no notice of us — so as a general argument for atheism it is a nonstarter. Even for Jews and Christians, who (rightly, Feser says) believe God does seek relationship, it leaves untouched the attributes the proofs establish — one, simple, purely actual, immutable, immaterial, eternal, omnipotent, omniscient — and if those hold, atheism is false. As for God’s goodness and love, the reply parallels the one to evil: given proof of a good and loving God, to whatever extent he hasn’t made himself more obvious there must be a greater good in it. There is no more reason to think such a good impossible here than with Rowe’s fawn — and even Rowe didn’t claim that.

John Hick suggested God keeps an **epistemic distance** so we are free to choose a relationship with him. Feser thinks Hick greatly exaggerates this: the universe isn’t religiously ambiguous, since there are decisive arguments, and free choice about God doesn’t depend on doubt — history is full of believers who did terrible things without doubting God. But there is a kernel of truth: God gives us a long leash in what we think as well as in what we do. Philosophers have denied change, time, matter, causation, free will, the self, even consciousness, so it is unsurprising some deny God. Finite minds err, free wills can turn attention away from evidence, and people have motives for doing so.

**Second assumption.** Is God really not obvious to most people? Few know philosophical theism, but historically the vast majority of humans have been theists of some kind, and most still are — whether monotheist, pantheist, polytheist, or holding a vaguer sense of the divine — often with a confidence atheists complain about. If God is hidden from most people, most people haven’t noticed. That their reasons are unsophisticated no more makes God hidden from them than a layman’s weak grasp of the evidence makes scientific truths hidden from him; ordinary belief in a divine cause of the world is often a simplified approximation of the proofs. Historically most experts — from Plato and Aristotle through Augustine, Avicenna, Aquinas, Descartes, Leibniz, and Newton — held that God’s existence can be known by argument, and many philosophers still do; to say their arguments have since been refuted begs the question. And intellectuals who reject theism on the basis of incompetent objections like “what caused God?” have no standing to fault ordinary believers’ evidence. Their sense that God is obviously hidden says more about their grasp of natural theology than about natural theology.
summary.takeaway: The hiddenness argument rests on two doubtful assumptions: that God would make himself obvious (not true of every theism, and defeated by greater-good reasoning given the proofs) and that he isn’t obvious (most people in history have found God anything but hidden).
summary.deepDive:
The trick to mastering this section is to hold the two assumptions apart, because Feser’s replies to each are quite different in kind.

**Assumption one: God would make himself obvious.** Schellenberg’s reasoning is that a perfectly loving God would want an explicit relationship with each person, which requires that person to believe he exists. Feser’s first move is logical: not every theism holds that God seeks a relationship with us — Aristotle’s Unmoved Mover eternally contemplates itself and pays us no attention. So hiddenness can’t be a completely general argument for atheism. His second move is about scope: even for Jews and Christians, who (rightly, Feser says) believe God does seek relationship, the argument leaves untouched most of what the proofs establish — one, simple, purely actual, immutable, immaterial, eternal, omnipotent, omniscient cause. That already refutes atheism. His third move mirrors the reply to Rowe: given proof of a loving God, any lack of obviousness must serve a greater good. There is no better reason to deny that possibility here than with the fawn.

Feser then weighs Hick’s idea of **epistemic distance**. He rejects two exaggerations — that the universe is religiously ambiguous, and that free choice about God requires doubt (history is full of believers who did evil without doubting God) — but keeps a kernel. God gives us a long leash in thought as in action. A thought experiment: list what intelligent philosophers have denied — change, time, the material world, causation, free will, the self, even consciousness. If minds can talk themselves out of *those*, it is no surprise some talk themselves out of God. Finite minds err; free wills choose where to look; and people have motives, a point Feser develops in the next section.

**Assumption two: God isn’t obvious.** Here the reply is largely empirical and historical. The vast majority of humans have affirmed some divine reality — monotheist, pantheist, polytheist, or vaguer — and often with a confidence atheists complain about. If God is hidden from most people, they haven’t noticed. The atheist may say ordinary believers’ reasons are weak; Feser answers with the layman’s grasp of science, which is real knowledge despite being crude. Most experts in Western history held God knowable by argument; saying their arguments have been refuted begs the question. And intellectuals who reject God via incompetent objections like “what caused God?” have little standing to accuse ordinary people of insufficient evidence.

People often think Feser is saying nonbelievers are dishonest. He isn’t: his explanation is finitude and freedom, which apply to everyone. In conversation with a sincere seeker, that is the note to strike.

checks.q: Why is Schellenberg’s argument a nonstarter against Aristotle’s theism?
options: Aristotle’s God does not seek a personal relationship with us, so the argument’s key premise doesn’t apply
Aristotle believed God was obvious
Aristotle was an atheist
Aristotle rejected free will
checks.explanation: The Unmoved Mover contemplates itself and ignores us, so the argument cannot be completely general.

checks.q: What kernel of truth does Feser find in Hick’s epistemic distance?
options: The universe is equally theistic and atheistic
Doubt is necessary for free choice
Finite minds and free wills allow people to err in what they think, just as in what they do
God deliberately hides from philosophers
checks.explanation: Feser rejects the ambiguity thesis and the doubt thesis but keeps the long-leash point.

checks.q: How does Feser answer the claim that God is hidden from most people?
options: He admits most people are atheists
He says only philosophers can know God
He appeals to miracles
He notes that most people in history have believed in some divine reality, so if God is hidden from them, they haven’t noticed
checks.explanation: Feser attacks the second assumption historically and with the layman-science analogy.

summary.plain: “If God existed, he’d make it obvious.” Feser questions both parts. Not every idea of God says he must make himself obvious, and if God is good there could be a good reason for some hiddenness. Also, most people in history have believed in God — so he hasn’t exactly been hidden.

summary.heading: Objection: theistic arguments are just rationalizations
summary.body:
Another popular way of avoiding the arguments is to say that they are not worth taking seriously because believers decided God exists first and only afterward went looking for reasons: the “proofs” are rationalizations of conclusions settled in advance.

Feser’s first reply is that this is a textbook **ad hominem** fallacy of the kind called **poisoning the well**: rejecting an argument because of some supposed vested interest or suspect motive of the person who offers it. As every logician knows, whether an argument is good or bad is completely independent of the motives or character of the person giving it. A valid argument with true premises is sound even if its author is a scoundrel; an invalid one is invalid even if its author is a saint.

His second reply is that the accusation can be turned around with equal justice. A person may want to believe in God and so be inclined to look for reasons for belief while avoiding hard scrutiny of atheist arguments. But a person may equally want *not* to believe in God and so look for reasons for atheism while avoiding hard scrutiny of the arguments for theism. Feser cites a remarkably candid admission from the atheist philosopher Thomas Nagel, who confessed that he wants atheism to be true, hopes there is no God, is made uneasy by how many intelligent people he knows are believers, and suspects that this “cosmic authority problem” is common and responsible for much of the scientism and reductionism of our time.

Feser is careful about what he draws from this. He does not say all atheists are intellectually dishonest — nor are all theists. His point is that honesty or dishonesty on either side is beside the point. What matters is whether the arguments are good, and that can be settled only by examining them, not by spending time hunting for excuses not to.
summary.takeaway: An argument’s soundness does not depend on the arguer’s motives; since the motive charge can be made against either side (Nagel admits hoping there is no God), the only way forward is to examine the arguments themselves.
summary.deepDive:
Why exactly are motives irrelevant to arguments? The cleanest way to see it is to distinguish two situations.

In the first, you rely on someone’s **testimony**: a witness says she saw the defendant at the scene. Here motives matter a great deal, because you cannot check what she saw; you are trusting her. If she stands to inherit from the victim, you should be wary.

In the second, someone offers you an **argument**: premises and a claimed logical connection to a conclusion. Here you do not have to trust the arguer at all, because you can check the premises and the logic yourself. Worked example: a biased accountant, who wants the company to look profitable, hands you the books. His bias is a reason to *check* the arithmetic carefully — but if the sums add up and the entries are accurate, the company is profitable, bias and all. And if they don’t, they don’t, even if an unbiased accountant had prepared them. The five proofs are like the books, not like testimony: every premise is on the table for inspection.

That is what makes poisoning the well a fallacy. It treats an argument as if it were testimony, and so replaces checking with suspicion. A close cousin is the **genetic fallacy** (a course term): judging a belief by how someone came to hold it rather than by whether it is true or well supported. Even if a believer first accepted God as a child, that tells us nothing about whether the Thomistic proof is valid.

Feser’s use of Nagel is often misunderstood. People think he quotes Nagel to show atheists are the ones really rationalizing. But Feser explicitly denies that all atheists are dishonest. The Nagel passage functions as a **symmetry** point: if motives could discredit arguments, they could discredit both sides, so appealing to them settles nothing. Once that is seen, both parties are thrown back on the only relevant question — is a premise false, or is the logic invalid?

This section also connects to the module’s argument at step 22: the motive charge is one of the “wrong standard” objections, judging demonstrations by something other than their premises and logic. In conversation, the best response is cheerful and brief: grant that you might have motives, grant that your critic might too, and ask which premise fails. That keeps the discussion on the only ground where it can be resolved.

checks.q: Which fallacy does Feser say the “rationalization” objection commits?
options: Begging the question
Poisoning the well, a form of ad hominem
Fallacy of composition
Special pleading
checks.explanation: It rejects arguments because of the arguer’s supposed motives rather than their content.

checks.q: What does Feser use Thomas Nagel’s confession to show?
options: That atheists are generally dishonest
That Nagel secretly believed in God
That the motive charge cuts both ways, so motives cannot settle whether arguments are good
That scientism is correct
checks.explanation: Feser explicitly says not all atheists are dishonest; the point is symmetry.

summary.plain: “You only believe these arguments because you want God to exist.” Feser says that’s beside the point: an argument is good or bad no matter why someone offers it. And the charge cuts both ways — one famous atheist admitted he hopes there’s no God.

summary.heading: Objection: it can’t be a proof if so many people remain unconvinced
summary.body:
Three problems.

1. Many standard criticisms of these arguments are incompetent, aimed at caricatures and ignorant of what defenders actually said. Rejection by ill-informed critics is no evidence that a demonstration fails.
2. **Double standard.** Skeptics treat the mere existence of an objection to a theistic argument as showing the argument “fails,” as if a good argument must win universal assent. They never treat arguments for materialism or against free will that way — there, critics are just part of ongoing debate, and the argument stays on the table. Even eccentric philosophical positions get that courtesy; theistic arguments don’t, and Hume’s having said something two centuries ago is treated as a final refutation. Feser quotes Hilary Putnam in a footnote noting that by the “must convince every rational person” standard, the philosophical arguments of Frege, Russell, Quine, Davidson, and Lewis would all fail too.
3. Critics misunderstand what classical theists mean by **demonstration**: a conclusion that follows with deductive necessity from premises that are certain, their certainty established by metaphysical analysis. That makes it more secure than scientific inference in two respects: it is not probabilistic or an inference to the best explanation where an alternative might in principle be right; and its premises can’t be overturned by future empirical inquiry, because every possible inquiry presupposes them.

The Aristotelian proof illustrates: its first premise, that change occurs, is empirical in a sense (so the argument isn’t a priori), but no future experience could overturn it, because any future experience would itself be a change. We might empirically show a particular apparent change unreal, but not that all change is. The other premises (the principle of causality, the impossibility of an infinite hierarchical regress) are defended by metaphysical argument — e.g., causality follows from PSR, which can be defended by showing its denial is self-undermining. The other four proofs can be defended similarly.

Such arguments are ambitious, but nothing in their strategy implies every reader — even a fair-minded, informed one — will immediately see their force, or that no hard philosophical work is needed to defend the premises. Controversy does not entail failure. What a demonstration requires is that, when all is said and done, it can be defended against every objection claiming the conclusion doesn’t follow or a premise is doubtful. Feser claims the book has done that for all five proofs, and closes the book with the traditional sign-off of a completed proof: Q.E.D.
summary.takeaway: A demonstration is a valid deduction from certain premises that no future observation could overturn; it need not compel instant universal assent, so the existence of critics shows controversy, not failure.
summary.deepDive:
This final section tells you what the whole book has been claiming: that the proofs are **demonstrations**.

What it is: an argument whose conclusion follows with deductive necessity from premises that are certain, where the certainty of the premises is established by metaphysical analysis. Feser says this gives knowledge more secure than scientific inference in two respects. First, it isn’t probabilistic or an inference to the best explanation, where a rival hypothesis might in principle turn out correct. Second, its premises cannot be overturned by further empirical inquiry, because they concern what any possible inquiry presupposes.

The Aristotelian proof shows how the second point works. Its first premise — change occurs — is empirical in a sense: we know it from experience, so the proof is not a priori. Yet run a thought experiment: imagine some future observation that would show there is no change at all. Making the observation would itself be a change (in your perceptions, in your instruments). So no future experience could refute the premise. You can coherently doubt that *this* apparent change is real (maybe it’s an illusion), but not that change as such is real. The other premises — that potentials are actualized only by what is actual, and that hierarchical series cannot regress infinitely — are defended by argument: the principle of causality follows from PSR, and PSR is defended by showing its denial undermines itself (a reductio).

What a demonstration is not: a device that forces agreement from everyone who hears it. Feser stresses that nothing in the strategy implies every reader, even a fair and informed one, will immediately see the force of the argument, or that no hard work is needed to defend its premises. Mathematics offers a parallel: many proofs took years for competent mathematicians to accept, and some people never follow them — without that making them non-proofs.

The double standard is the other half of the section. Arguments for materialism or against free will have critics too, but no one says they have therefore “failed”; they remain on the table. Putnam, in the passage Feser quotes, noted that if a sound proof had to convince every rational person, the philosophical arguments of Frege, Russell, Quine, Davidson, and Lewis would all fail.

People often think Q.E.D. at the end is triumphalism. It is better read as a claim with a standard attached: a demonstration succeeds when it can be defended against every objection that the conclusion doesn’t follow or a premise is doubtful. That is the standard the whole of chapter 7 has been trying to meet, and the reason this module’s argument ends at step 23 with the burden on the critic.

checks.q: Why can no future experience overturn the premise that change occurs?
options: Because any future experience would itself be an instance of change
Because it is known a priori
Because physics has confirmed it
Because Aristotle defined it that way
checks.explanation: The premise is empirical but self-confirming in any possible experience; we can doubt particular changes, not change as such.

checks.q: According to Feser, what does a demonstration need in order to succeed?
options: Immediate assent from every rational hearer
Endorsement by most living philosophers
Empirical confirmation
The ability to be defended against every objection claiming the conclusion doesn’t follow or a premise is doubtful
checks.explanation: Controversy does not entail failure; defensibility against all objections is the standard.

checks.q: Which of the following best illustrates the double standard Feser describes?
options: Rejecting astrology because it makes false predictions
Treating any objection to a theistic argument as showing it fails, while keeping arguments for materialism on the table despite their critics
Asking for evidence before accepting a claim
Preferring simpler explanations
checks.explanation: The complaint is not high standards but uniquely severe ones applied only to arguments for God (Putnam’s point).

terms: The five proofs (Aristotelian, Neo-Platonic, Augustinian, Thomistic, rationalist)
summary.plain: “It can’t be a real proof if so many smart people disagree.” Feser answers that every serious argument in philosophy has critics, and nobody says those arguments automatically fail. A proof, in his sense, is a tight chain of reasoning from certain starting points — and it succeeds if it survives every objection, not if everyone instantly agrees.

argument.name: The Case Against Scientism — and the Diagnostic Pattern Behind the Popular Objections
argument.overview:
This half-chapter has no single formal proof. Its main line of reasoning is Feser’s case against **scientism**, the premise that quietly powers most of the popular objections (if only science yields knowledge, metaphysical demonstrations can be dismissed unread). The reasoning below reconstructs that case in Feser’s own order — the self-refutation dilemma, the limits of scientific description, the limits of scientific explanation, and the failure of the argument from success — and then states the general **diagnostic pattern** Feser applies to the remaining objections.

Stages 1–4 show scientism has no support and decisive evidence against it. Stage 5 draws the consequence: the five proofs have to be met on their own terms — false premise, invalid inference, or begged question — and the other popular objections fail because they either refute themselves, attack a caricature of God as one more complex being or hypothesis, or evaluate demonstrations by standards (probability, parsimony, universal assent, motive) that do not apply to them.

stages.title: Stage 1 — The dilemma: self-refuting or trivial
stages.gist: Scientism is not a scientific claim and science rests on and needs philosophy; stretching “science” to include philosophy makes scientism empty and lets natural theology in.

stages.title: Stage 2 — The limits of scientific description
stages.gist: Physics captures only quantifiable structure by methodological choice, so it cannot describe all of reality — and its own structural description implies there is more.

stages.title: Stage 3 — The limits of scientific explanation
stages.gist: On every theory of laws, laws cannot be the ultimate explanation; saying there is no ultimate explanation is philosophy, and false by PSR.

stages.title: Stage 4 — The argument from success and the fallbacks fail
stages.gist: Predictive success shows usefulness for the predictable, not that nothing else exists; the “worth knowing” and “conceptual analysis” retreats are themselves self-undermining philosophy.

stages.title: Stage 5 — The diagnostic pattern
stages.gist: With scientism gone, the proofs must be engaged directly; the remaining popular objections fail by self-refutation, caricature, or wrong standards.

steps.text: Scientism is the thesis that science is the only genuine source of knowledge, so that any legitimate metaphysics is just whatever is implicit in science.
steps.why: Feser’s definition; he cites Rosenberg’s version, which says science’s methods are the only reliable ways of knowing anything. It is what lets critics dismiss natural theology as “unscientific” without examining it.
steps.example: Rosenberg’s version: the methods of science are the only reliable ways to secure knowledge of anything. On this view, “God exists” can’t be known because no experiment tests it.
steps.challenge: Isn’t this a straw man — does anyone really hold such a strong view?
steps.answer: Rosenberg states and embraces it in so many words, and Feser notes it is a key ingredient of the New Atheism. The “modest” version (science is merely the best method) is handled in the module’s objection on weak scientism.

steps.text: The thesis of scientism is not itself a result of scientific method; no experiment or observation establishes it.
steps.why: It is a claim *about* science and knowledge in general — a philosophical claim. Not even the weaker claim that science is a rational form of inquiry can be established scientifically.
steps.example: No laboratory result, telescope observation, or equation has the conclusion “only science yields knowledge.” It is a claim about all inquiry, made from outside any particular science.
steps.challenge: Couldn’t the thesis be supported by the historical track record of science?
steps.answer: That is the argument from success (steps 15–16), which Feser shows is invalid. And an argument from history about the scope of knowledge is itself philosophical reasoning, not a scientific result.

steps.text: Science rests on presuppositions it cannot justify without circularity: that there is an objective, mind-independent world, that it has law-like regularities, and that our senses and intellect can grasp them.
steps.why: Every scientific procedure already assumes these, so using science to prove them would argue in a circle.
steps.example: To trust a thermometer reading, you must already assume there is a real temperature outside your mind, that it behaves regularly, and that your eyes read the dial correctly — none of which the reading itself proves.
steps.challenge: Can’t science confirm these presuppositions gradually, by the success of predictions built on them?
steps.answer: Every such confirmation is interpreted using the very presuppositions in question, so it argues in a circle. Their justification has to come from an extrascientific vantage point.

steps.text: So justifying science — and all the more, showing that only science tracks reality — requires an extrascientific standpoint, whose very existence falsifies scientism.
steps.why: From 2 and 3. This is the first horn: taken strictly, scientism refutes itself.
steps.example: A philosopher reflecting on perception and knowledge concludes that our senses do put us in touch with a real, orderly world. That reflection is not an experiment — and its existence shows science isn’t the only rational route to reality.
steps.challenge: Maybe the presuppositions are just pragmatic assumptions that need no justification.
steps.answer: Then science’s claim to reveal reality rests on unjustified assumptions, which undercuts scientism’s claim that science alone gives knowledge. Either way, science’s standing depends on something beyond science.

steps.text: Science also depends on philosophy to interpret its results: whether reality is made of substances or events, what causation is, what the universals in laws are, and whether theories describe reality or merely predict.
steps.why: Scientific findings bear on these questions but cannot settle them. So science needs philosophy at both ends — to justify its starting points and to interpret its conclusions (Kekes: philosophy is the better paradigm of rationality).
steps.example: Two physicists agree on every equation of quantum mechanics but disagree on whether the theory describes reality or is just a prediction tool. No further experiment settles it; it is a philosophical question.
steps.challenge: Maybe these interpretive questions are meaningless and science doesn’t need them answered.
steps.answer: Declaring them meaningless is itself a philosophical position needing defense. And whether science describes reality at all is exactly what scientism needs answered in its favor.

steps.text: If the defender of scientism responds by counting philosophy as “science,” the term now covers anything that could be offered as evidence, including natural theology.
steps.why: Aristotle and Aquinas called natural theology a science — more certain than physics because it demonstrates from premises every physical science presupposes. A stretched definition has no non-arbitrary way to exclude it.
steps.example: Aquinas treats natural theology as a *scientia* — demonstrated knowledge from certain principles — and holds it more certain than physics because its premises (that things change, exist contingently) are what physics presupposes.
steps.challenge: Surely “science” just means the empirical sciences, so natural theology can’t qualify.
steps.answer: If “science” means only the empirical sciences, we are back on the first horn and scientism is self-refuting. The defender can’t have both a narrow definition that excludes natural theology and a broad one that saves scientism.

steps.text: Therefore scientism is either self-refuting (narrow version) or vacuous (broad version); either way it cannot justify dismissing natural theology unheard.
steps.why: From 4 and 6. This is the dilemma. The critic must face the arguments head-on instead of declaring them out of bounds.
steps.example: A critic who says “I needn’t read Feser, his arguments aren’t scientific” is using scientism as a dismissal device. The dilemma shows the device either breaks or cuts nothing.

steps.text: The method of physics deliberately restricts attention to what can be described mathematically and so predicted and controlled.
steps.why: Following Galileo’s image of nature as a book written in mathematics. That restriction is the source of physics’ success — and of its blind spots.
steps.example: Galileo’s image of nature as a book written in mathematics: physics attends to mass, charge, position, and their equations, and sets aside everything that can’t be so expressed.
steps.challenge: Isn’t mathematical description simply the most accurate description there is?
steps.answer: It is extremely precise for what it captures. But precision about quantities is not completeness; the method selects its subject matter in advance, so what it leaves out isn’t thereby shown to be less real.

steps.text: Features left out of a description by the method’s design are not thereby shown to be absent from reality.
steps.why: The airplane engineers’ passenger-weight calculations say nothing about meal or movie preferences, but that is because weight is all the method looks at — not because preferences don’t exist. Qualities, thoughts, purposes and meanings fall through physics’ net the same way.
steps.example: The airline engineers’ data ignore passengers’ meal and movie preferences. It would be absurd to conclude the passengers have none; the method guaranteed the data would be silent.
steps.challenge: Perhaps the omitted features really are unreal, and physics’ silence reflects that.
steps.answer: Maybe for some particular feature, but that would need a separate argument. Silence produced by a method’s design can’t by itself be evidence of absence, which is the point of Feser’s remark that the method stipulates the omission.

steps.text: Physics tells us the abstract mathematical structure of events, not the intrinsic nature of what has that structure.
steps.why: Bertrand Russell, no friend of theism, emphasized exactly this: physics is silent about what it is that changes.
steps.example: Russell: physics lays down equations for the logical structure of events but leaves completely unknown the intrinsic character of what has the structure — like chess notation that says nothing about what the pieces are made of.
steps.challenge: Maybe there is nothing more to the physical world than its mathematical structure.
steps.answer: Structure is a pattern of relations, and relations need relata. Feser’s point is that there is no such thing as structure all by itself; something must have it.

steps.text: So physics cannot give a complete description even of physical reality; indeed, it implies there is more to reality than it describes.
steps.why: From 8–10: there is no structure without something that has the structure, so the structural description itself points beyond itself.
steps.example: Because physics tells us that a mathematically describable structure exists, it implicitly tells us that something bears that structure — something whose intrinsic nature physics doesn’t reveal.
steps.challenge: Couldn’t future physics discover the intrinsic nature?
steps.answer: Not while remaining the mathematical-structural discipline it is. The limitation is one of method, not of current progress.

steps.text: Scientific explanation works by appeal to laws of nature, which leaves open what a law is, how it can do anything, and why these laws hold.
steps.why: Any scientific explanation presupposes the laws it uses, so it cannot answer these questions about the laws themselves (the problem with Krauss’ “layers” of laws).
steps.example: Krauss appeals to laws of quantum gravity and then to “layers” of laws; each appeal invites the question of what those laws are and why they hold.
steps.challenge: Isn’t asking why the laws hold just asking too much of science?
steps.answer: Yes — which is exactly Feser’s point. The question is legitimate but not scientific, because scientific explanation presupposes the laws it uses; answering it requires philosophy.

steps.text: On every main theory of laws, laws cannot be the ultimate explanation of the world.
steps.why: Aristotelian laws presuppose the things whose natures they describe; Cartesian-Newtonian laws make God the real explainer; Humean laws merely redescribe regularities; Platonic laws still leave unexplained why a world participates in them, and in these rather than others.
steps.example: On the Humean view, “it is a law that A’s are followed by B’s” means only that A’s are regularly followed by B’s — so “why?” is answered by restating the pattern.
steps.challenge: Perhaps there is some fifth theory of laws on which they could be ultimate.
steps.answer: Any law presupposes the things it governs or something that grounds it; Feser’s survey covers the main options, and none escapes this. The burden would be on the critic to specify the alternative.

steps.text: So the ultimate explanation of things, if there is one, lies beyond science — and the claim that there is none is itself philosophical, and false.
steps.why: From 12–13. Denying ultimate explanation is not a scientific result, and it violates the principle of sufficient reason defended in chapter 5.
steps.example: Saying “there simply is no ultimate explanation” is not the result of any measurement; it is a claim about reality as a whole — and PSR (chapter 5) rules it out.
steps.challenge: Why accept PSR, when some physicists say quantum events have no cause?
steps.answer: Part A answered the quantum objection, and chapter 5 defended PSR, including by showing that denying it undermines the very rationality of inquiry. The denial is also philosophical, not scientific.

steps.text: The main argument for scientism is that science’s predictive and technological success is unmatched, so what science reveals is probably all that is real.
steps.why: Feser’s two-step reconstruction of Rosenberg’s argument, generalized to include sciences beyond physics.
steps.example: Rosenberg: the phenomenal accuracy of physics’ predictions and the power of its technology are powerful reasons to believe physics is the whole truth about reality.
steps.challenge: Isn’t it reasonable to trust the method that has worked best?
steps.answer: Trusting it within its domain is reasonable, and Feser does. What doesn’t follow is that its domain is everything (step 16).

steps.text: An argument of exactly that form is invalid: the success of a method at detecting one kind of thing does not make it probable that nothing else exists.
steps.why: Metal detectors outperform every other method at finding metal, yet that doesn’t show metal is all there is. Replying that science, unlike metal detectors, covers the whole of reality begs the question. Demanding the predictive successes of metaphysics is like demanding the metal-detecting successes of gardening.
steps.example: Metal detectors outperform every other method at finding metal, yet no one concludes metal is probably all that exists. Likewise demanding metaphysics’ predictions is like demanding the metal-detecting record of a spatula.
steps.challenge: The analogy fails because science, unlike a detector, is aimed at all of reality.
steps.answer: That reply assumes precisely what is in question — whether science covers all of reality — and so begs the question.

steps.text: The retreat that science at least tells us everything worth knowing is both question-begging and itself a non-scientific claim.
steps.why: It is like taking only easy classes and boasting of your GPA: if only the predictable and consensus-generating counts as science, success is guaranteed trivially. And the claim that only such questions matter is philosophy.
steps.example: The student who takes only courses he knows he’ll ace and boasts of his GPA: if only predictable, consensus-yielding questions count as “science,” its perfect record is guaranteed.
steps.challenge: But philosophy really doesn’t achieve consensus, so isn’t it reasonable to discount it?
steps.answer: Lack of consensus shows a question is hard, not unimportant or unanswerable — and the claim that only consensus-yielding questions matter is itself a philosophical claim needing defense.

steps.text: The claim that any non-scientific inquiry is mere “conceptual analysis” is a version of Hume’s Fork and refutes itself, while logic and mathematics fit neither category.
steps.why: The dichotomy is neither a conceptual truth nor a scientific finding. Logical and mathematical truths are necessary (unlike science) and objective (unlike mere concept-mapping). Natural theology’s conclusions fall between the tines the same way.
steps.example: “7 + 5 = 12” is necessary (it couldn’t have been otherwise, unlike the boiling point of water) and objective (true even if nobody conceived it), so it fits neither “science” nor “mere conceptual analysis.”
steps.challenge: Maybe logic and mathematics are really empirical generalizations or conventions after all.
steps.answer: Chapter 3 shows the serious difficulties with such views, and Feser notes the only motive for adopting them here is to rescue scientism — which makes the move ad hoc.

steps.text: Therefore there is no good argument for scientism and decisive arguments against it.
steps.why: From 7, 11, 14 and 15–18: its supporting argument fails and it faces self-refutation, incompleteness of description, and incompleteness of explanation.
steps.example: After the dilemma, the limits of description and explanation, and the failure of the success argument, scientism has no remaining support and several decisive problems.

steps.text: So the five proofs — which begin from what any possible science must presuppose (change, composition, contingency, the distinction of essence and existence, abstract truths) — can only be rebutted by showing a false premise, an invalid step, or a begged question.
steps.why: With scientism gone there is no shortcut. They are attempted strict demonstrations, not hypotheses to be weighed for probability or parsimony.
steps.example: To answer the Aristotelian proof, a critic must show, say, that change doesn’t require actualization by something actual, or that a hierarchical series could regress infinitely — not merely that the proof is “unscientific.”
steps.challenge: Couldn’t a critic reject the proofs simply because they are unfalsifiable by experiment?
steps.answer: That objection presupposes scientism, now defeated. The proofs are falsifiable in the relevant sense: show a premise false or an inference invalid.

steps.text: Many popular objections undermine themselves or rest on arbitrary stipulation — scientism, Hume’s Fork, and the claim that the fundamental laws are a brute fact.
steps.why: The brute-fact view contradicts PSR, has no motive except avoiding the proofs, and would drain all higher-level laws of explanatory power (the shelf with brackets let go in midair).
steps.example: The brute-fact view: it contradicts PSR, has no motive except avoiding theism, and leaves higher laws explaining nothing — the shelf whose brackets are let go in midair.
steps.challenge: Isn’t it just intellectual honesty to admit that some things may have no explanation?
steps.answer: Not when an explanation has been offered and not refuted (Gerson’s point), and not when the admission would drain all other explanations of force. Honesty requires engaging the proposed explanation.

steps.text: Others attack a caricature of God as one more complex being or hypothesis, or judge demonstrations by standards that do not apply to them — probability, universal assent, or the arguer’s motives.
steps.why: The complex-designer and one-god-further objections misdescribe the simple, purely actual God the proofs reach; Rowe’s and Schellenberg’s arguments are defeated by independent proof of a good God; poisoning the well and “people still disagree” are irrelevant to validity and soundness.
steps.example: “Who designed the designer?” assumes a composite God the proofs deny; “one god further” puts God in a genus; “people disagree” judges a demonstration by universal assent; “you just want God” judges it by motive.
steps.challenge: Isn’t it convenient to say every objection misunderstands the view?
steps.answer: The diagnosis is checkable case by case: the proofs explicitly conclude to a simple, purely actual cause, and the classical conception long predates these objections. Where an objection engages that view, Feser answers it directly.

steps.text: Hence none of the popular objections overturns the five proofs; the burden stays on the critic to engage the demonstrations themselves.
steps.why: From 19–22. This is the chapter’s — and the book’s — closing verdict: the proofs can be defended against every objection claiming the conclusion doesn’t follow or a premise is doubtful.
steps.example: Feser closes the book with Q.E.D.: the proofs, he claims, have been defended against every objection claiming the conclusion doesn’t follow or a premise is doubtful.
steps.challenge: Isn’t declaring victory premature while many philosophers still reject the proofs?
steps.answer: Controversy isn’t failure (section on demonstration). The claim is that no objection actually succeeds; the way to contest it is to name a premise and show it false.

keyTerms.definition: The view that science is the only genuine source of knowledge, so that philosophy is legitimate only insofar as it is implicit in science.
keyTerms.example: “If it can’t be tested in a lab, it isn’t knowledge” — a claim that itself can’t be tested in a lab.
keyTerms.origin: From Latin *scientia*, “knowledge.” As a critical label it became common in the twentieth century (e.g., Hayek); Feser applies it to the New Atheists and to Rosenberg, who embraces the label.
keyTerms.confuseWith: Science — science is a set of methods for studying the measurable; scientism is a philosophical thesis that those methods are the only route to knowledge.

keyTerms.definition: A claim that, if true, would undermine the grounds for accepting it.
keyTerms.example: Scientism is not a scientific result, so by its own standard it isn’t knowledge.
keyTerms.origin: A standard notion in logic (Greek *peritropē*, “turning around,” was the ancient term for turning a thesis against itself).
keyTerms.confuseWith: A false claim — a self-refuting claim isn’t merely false; asserting or accepting it undermines the very grounds for accepting it.

keyTerms.definition: The version of scientism that escapes self-refutation by redefining “science” to include philosophy — so that it no longer excludes anything, natural theology included.
keyTerms.example: “Philosophy is just very abstract science” — then Aquinas’ natural theology counts as science too.
keyTerms.origin: Feser’s name for the second horn of his dilemma against scientism.
keyTerms.confuseWith: Moderate scientism — moderate scientism still excludes some inquiries as non-knowledge; vacuous scientism has stretched “science” so far it excludes nothing, natural theology included.

keyTerms.definition: Assumptions science must make but cannot prove without circularity: a mind-independent world, law-like regularities, and the reliability of our cognitive faculties.
keyTerms.example: No experiment can prove that experiments tell us about an external world; every experiment assumes it.
keyTerms.origin: A theme of the philosophy of science generally; Feser’s list echoes classical realist and Aristotelian discussions.
keyTerms.confuseWith: Scientific hypotheses — hypotheses are tested by science; presuppositions are what any test already assumes and so cannot be tested without circularity.

keyTerms.definition: Deliberately attending only to certain features of a thing for a purpose, and ignoring the rest.
keyTerms.example: Airplane engineers treat passengers as average weights; physics treats nature as mathematical structure.
keyTerms.origin: Latin *abstrahere*, “to draw away”: considering one aspect of a thing apart from the rest. A central notion in Aristotelian-Thomistic accounts of how the sciences work.
keyTerms.confuseWith: Denial — abstracting from a feature means setting it aside for a purpose, not claiming it doesn’t exist.

keyTerms.definition: Physics tells us the mathematical relations among events (structure) but not what the things having those relations are in themselves.
keyTerms.example: Russell: physics gives equations for changes but is silent about what it is that changes.
keyTerms.origin: Bertrand Russell, *My Philosophical Development* and *The Analysis of Matter*; today associated with structural realism.
keyTerms.confuseWith: Appearance vs. reality — the point isn’t that physics describes mere appearances, but that it describes real relations without saying what the related things are in themselves.

keyTerms.definition: Aristotelian (descriptions of how things act given their natures), Cartesian-Newtonian (God’s decrees for regular behavior), Humean (summaries of observed regularities), Platonic (abstract objects things participate in). On none can laws be the ultimate explanation.
keyTerms.example: A Humean law that A’s are followed by B’s tells you *that* the pattern holds, not *why*.
keyTerms.origin: Aristotelian (natures/essences), Cartesian-Newtonian (divine decree), Humean (regularity theory, from David Hume), Platonic (abstract objects, after Plato’s Forms).
keyTerms.confuseWith: Causes — on the Aristotelian and Humean views especially, laws are descriptions of how causes behave, not additional causes that make things happen.

keyTerms.definition: The inference from science’s unmatched predictive and technological success to the conclusion that what science reveals is probably all that is real.
keyTerms.example: Rosenberg: the reliability of technology shows physics is the whole truth. Feser: compare metal detectors.
keyTerms.origin: Feser’s reconstruction of Alex Rosenberg’s argument in *The Atheist’s Guide to Reality*.
keyTerms.confuseWith: The “no miracles” argument for scientific realism — that argument says science’s success shows its theories are roughly true; Rosenberg’s version jumps further, to the claim that science tells the *whole* truth.

keyTerms.definition: Assuming in your argument the very point in dispute.
keyTerms.example: Saying science differs from a metal detector because science detects all of reality — which is exactly what is at issue.
keyTerms.origin: A mistranslation of Latin *petitio principii*, “assuming the starting point” — Aristotle’s fallacy of assuming what is to be proved.
keyTerms.confuseWith: Raising the question — in logic, begging the question means assuming the conclusion, not prompting someone to ask it.

keyTerms.definition: Hume’s thesis that every object of inquiry is either a relation of ideas (conceptual truth) or a matter of fact (empirical). It is itself neither, so it refutes itself.
keyTerms.example: Ladyman and Ross’s “science or mere conceptual analysis” is a modern version.
keyTerms.origin: David Hume, *An Enquiry Concerning Human Understanding*, section 4; the name “fork” was given by later commentators.
keyTerms.confuseWith: The analytic/synthetic distinction — related (and descended from it), but Hume’s Fork adds the sweeping claim that these two categories exhaust all knowledge.

keyTerms.definition: Philosophy understood as mapping how our concepts relate, which critics say may tell us only how we think, not how the world is.
keyTerms.example: Scientism’s advocates claim non-naturalized metaphysics is just this; Feser calls that a false alternative.
keyTerms.origin: Associated with twentieth-century analytic philosophy (G. E. Moore, ordinary language philosophy); used pejoratively by naturalists like Ladyman and Ross.
keyTerms.confuseWith: Metaphysics as classically understood — Aristotelian metaphysics claims to know the real features of being (act, potency, essence), not merely our concepts.

keyTerms.definition: The program (Ladyman and Ross) of treating metaphysics as nothing more than an extension of the natural sciences.
keyTerms.example: Their book title declares that every thing must go — only what science posits stays.
keyTerms.origin: James Ladyman and Don Ross (with Spurrett and Collier), *Every Thing Must Go* (2007), extending W. V. Quine’s “naturalized epistemology.”
keyTerms.confuseWith: Philosophy of science — philosophy of science studies science; naturalized metaphysics claims metaphysics should be nothing but an extension of science.

keyTerms.definition: A fact with no explanation of any kind — not in itself, not in anything else.
keyTerms.example: Mackie and Russell treat the fundamental laws of nature this way.
keyTerms.origin: A term popularized in twentieth-century analytic philosophy; the position is associated in Feser with J. L. Mackie and Bertrand Russell (in his 1948 debate with Copleston).
keyTerms.confuseWith: A self-explanatory fact — a brute fact has no explanation at all; the classical God is not a brute fact but explains himself, since his essence is to exist.

keyTerms.definition: Everything that exists has an explanation of its existence, either in its own nature or in something else (defended in chapter 5).
keyTerms.example: PSR rules out treating the fundamental laws as a brute fact.
keyTerms.origin: Named by Leibniz (*principium rationis sufficientis*); Feser defends an Aristotelian-Thomistic version in chapter 5.
keyTerms.confuseWith: The principle of causality — PSR says everything has an explanation (possibly in its own nature); the principle of causality says potentials are actualized only by something actual.

keyTerms.definition: A probabilistic argument from complex, precisely arranged natural structures, by analogy with artifacts, to an intelligent designer.
keyTerms.example: The eye or the bacterial flagellum. Feser insists the five proofs are not arguments of this type.
keyTerms.origin: William Paley, *Natural Theology* (1802), with his watch analogy; revived by the Intelligent Design movement (Behe’s bacterial flagellum).
keyTerms.confuseWith: Aquinas’s Fifth Way — the Fifth Way argues from the goal-directedness of even simple natural causes, not from complexity or probability (Feser treats this elsewhere).

keyTerms.definition: Having many parts that must be arranged just so for the thing to function.
keyTerms.example: Irrelevant to the Neo-Platonic proof, for which a pebble or a drop of water works as a starting point.
keyTerms.origin: Paley and the Intelligent Design literature (e.g., “irreducible complexity”).
keyTerms.confuseWith: Composition — the Neo-Platonic proof starts from composition (having parts of any kind, even a pebble’s), not from functional complexity.

keyTerms.definition: A deductively valid argument from premises known with certainty, whose certainty is shown by metaphysical analysis — not a probabilistic or best-explanation inference. To demonstrate a conclusion is to show it follows necessarily in this way; Feser calls the five proofs demonstrations.
keyTerms.example: The Aristotelian proof: change occurs; potentials are actualized only by the actual; hierarchical series can’t regress infinitely.
keyTerms.origin: Latin *demonstratio*, rendering Aristotle’s Greek *apodeixis*: a deduction yielding scientific knowledge from certain premises (*Posterior Analytics*).
keyTerms.confuseWith: Proof beyond reasonable doubt or a strong probabilistic case — a demonstration aims at necessity, not high probability.

keyTerms.definition: Reasoning to the hypothesis that best explains the evidence, weighed by parsimony and fit — always open to a better rival.
keyTerms.example: Why “a simpler explanation is more likely” misfires against a demonstration.
keyTerms.origin: The term “abduction” comes from C. S. Peirce; “inference to the best explanation” from Gilbert Harman (1965).
keyTerms.confuseWith: Deduction — deduction guarantees its conclusion if the premises are true; abduction only supports the best available hypothesis, which a better rival could displace.

keyTerms.definition: Treating something as a member of a category it does not belong to.
keyTerms.example: Treating triangularity as one more (invisible, well-drawn) triangle; treating God as one more god.
keyTerms.origin: Gilbert Ryle, *The Concept of Mind* (1949): the visitor who sees the colleges and libraries and asks where the university is.
keyTerms.confuseWith: A false belief within a category — a category mistake isn’t getting a fact wrong about a kind of thing, but treating something as belonging to the wrong kind altogether.

keyTerms.definition: Classical theism’s God: not a being that has and receives existence, but existence itself, from which all beings derive theirs.
keyTerms.example: Why God is not “a being” alongside Zeus and Thor.
keyTerms.origin: Latin, “subsisting being itself”: Aquinas’s description of God (e.g., *Summa Theologiae* I, q. 4, a. 2).
keyTerms.confuseWith: The Supreme Being — thinking of God as the greatest item on a list of beings misses the point; he is not an item on the list but the source of the being of everything on it.

keyTerms.definition: An argument that evil is logically compatible with God’s existence, without claiming to know God’s specific reasons for permitting it.
keyTerms.example: Feser’s reply to Mackie and Rowe.
keyTerms.origin: Contemporary usage popularized by Alvin Plantinga (*God, Freedom, and Evil*, 1974).
keyTerms.confuseWith: Theodicy — a defense shows compatibility; a theodicy claims to identify God’s actual reasons.

keyTerms.definition: In contemporary usage, an account of why God actually permits evil. (Older Thomistic works used the word for natural theology in general.)
keyTerms.example: Hick’s soul-making theodicy.
keyTerms.origin: Coined by Leibniz (*Théodicée*, 1710) from Greek *theos* “God” + *dikē* “justice”: justifying God. Older Thomists used it for natural theology in general.
keyTerms.confuseWith: Defense — a theodicy offers God’s actual reasons for evil; a defense only shows that some such reasons could exist.

keyTerms.definition: The claim that God and evil are strictly inconsistent.
keyTerms.example: Mackie: an omnipotent, good being would eliminate all evil; evil exists; so no such being.
keyTerms.origin: Classically posed by Epicurus as reported by Lactantius and Hume; the modern version is J. L. Mackie’s “Evil and Omnipotence” (1955).
keyTerms.confuseWith: The evidential problem — the logical version claims strict contradiction; the evidential version claims only improbability.

keyTerms.definition: The claim that evil, though consistent with God, makes God’s existence improbable.
keyTerms.example: Rowe’s fawn dying for days in a forest fire.
keyTerms.origin: William Rowe, “The Problem of Evil and Some Varieties of Atheism” (1979).
keyTerms.confuseWith: The existential problem of evil — the evidential problem is an argument about probability; the existential problem is the lived anguish of suffering, which calls for pastoral response more than argument.

keyTerms.definition: John Hick’s theme that confronting suffering and evil develops virtues and character.
keyTerms.example: Courage needs danger; compassion needs misfortune.
keyTerms.origin: John Hick, *Evil and the God of Love* (1966), borrowing the phrase from John Keats’s “vale of soul-making” and drawing on Irenaeus.
keyTerms.confuseWith: Punishment — soul-making sees suffering as an occasion for growth in virtue, not as a penalty for sin.

keyTerms.definition: The argument (Schellenberg) that a God seeking relationship with us would make his existence obvious, so the lack of obviousness counts against him.
keyTerms.example: Rests on two assumptions Feser rejects.
keyTerms.origin: J. L. Schellenberg, *Divine Hiddenness and Human Reason* (1993); the phrase echoes Isaiah 45:15, “a God who hides himself.”
keyTerms.confuseWith: The problem of evil — hiddenness concerns God’s existence not being evident; evil concerns suffering and wrongdoing. Feser answers both with parallel greater-good reasoning.

keyTerms.definition: Hick’s idea that God keeps his existence less than evident so we can freely choose a relationship with him.
keyTerms.example: Feser: Hick exaggerates it, but finite minds and free will do give us a long leash in what we think.
keyTerms.origin: John Hick, from Greek *epistēmē*, “knowledge”: a distance in knowledge, not in space.
keyTerms.confuseWith: Religious ambiguity — Hick also claimed the universe is equally readable theistically or atheistically; Feser accepts a modest epistemic distance but rejects that ambiguity.

keyTerms.definition: An ad hominem fallacy: dismissing an argument by pointing to the arguer’s alleged motives or vested interests.
keyTerms.example: “You only believe the proofs because you already wanted God.”
keyTerms.origin: Named by John Henry Newman (1864) after the medieval libel that Jews poisoned wells; a species of the *ad hominem* fallacy.
keyTerms.confuseWith: Legitimate questioning of testimony — a witness’s motives can matter when we rely on his say-so, but an argument’s soundness can be checked directly, regardless of who offers it.

keyTerms.definition: Thomas Nagel’s name for the wish that there be no God, which he admitted in himself and suspected drives much scientism and reductionism.
keyTerms.example: Shows the motive charge can cut both ways — and so decides nothing.
keyTerms.origin: Thomas Nagel, *The Last Word* (1997).
keyTerms.confuseWith: An argument for atheism — Nagel describes a desire, not a reason; Feser cites it only to show the motive charge cuts both ways.

keyTerms.definition: Treating any objection to a theistic argument as proof it “fails,” while treating arguments for materialism or against free will as live despite their critics.
keyTerms.example: Putnam: by the “convince every rational person” standard, Frege’s and Quine’s philosophical arguments fail too.
keyTerms.origin: Feser’s charge, supported by Hilary Putnam’s “Thoughts Addressed to an Analytical Thomist” (1997).
keyTerms.confuseWith: Reasonable caution — high standards for all ambitious arguments would be fine; the complaint is applying uniquely severe standards only to theistic ones.

keyTerms.definition: The early twenty-first-century popular movement (Dawkins, Dennett, Harris, Hitchens, and others) that attacked religion aggressively, often assuming that science alone yields knowledge.
keyTerms.example: Dawkins’ “who designed the designer?” and “one god further” are New Atheist staples that Feser answers in this chapter.
keyTerms.origin: Label coined by journalist Gary Wolf in *Wired* (2006).
keyTerms.confuseWith: Atheism in general — many academic atheists (Mackie, Nagel, Rowe) argue very differently and more carefully than the New Atheists.

keyTerms.definition: Knowledge of God’s existence and nature attainable by unaided human reason, apart from divine revelation.
keyTerms.example: The five proofs and the derivation of God’s attributes in chapter 6 are natural theology; the doctrine of the Trinity is not.
keyTerms.origin: Latin *theologia naturalis*; the ancient Stoic and Varronian division distinguished it from mythical and civil theology.
keyTerms.confuseWith: Revealed theology — revealed theology starts from scripture and tradition; natural theology from premises any rational person can assess.

keyTerms.definition: The traditional conception of God as absolutely simple, immutable, eternal, purely actual, necessary, and identical with his own existence.
keyTerms.example: Feser lists Aristotle, Plotinus, Augustine, Maimonides, Avicenna, Aquinas, and Leibniz as its representatives when answering “one god further.”
keyTerms.origin: Modern label for the mainstream view of pagan, Jewish, Christian, and Muslim philosophical theology.
keyTerms.confuseWith: Theistic personalism (neo-theism) — which pictures God as a very powerful person who changes, has parts or properties distinct from himself, and exists alongside other beings.

keyTerms.definition: The doctrine that God has no parts of any kind — not physical parts, nor a distinction of essence and existence, genus and difference, or substance and attributes. A being with no parts is called simple or noncomposite.
keyTerms.example: Because God is simple, he is not a member of the genus “gods,” and he is not the “complex designer” of Dawkins’ objection.
keyTerms.origin: Developed by Plotinus (“the One”), Augustine, and Aquinas; defended in chapters 2 and 6.
keyTerms.confuseWith: Simplicity meaning “easy to understand” — divine simplicity is about lacking composition, and God remains incomprehensible to us.

keyTerms.definition: Being wholly actual, with no unrealized potential; the Aristotelian proof’s description of the first cause. Such a being is described as purely actual.
keyTerms.example: In the brute-fact reply, only something purely actual can impart explanatory power without deriving it.
keyTerms.origin: Latin, “pure act,” from Aristotle’s *energeia*; used by Aquinas.
keyTerms.confuseWith: Being very active or busy — pure act means complete actuality of being, not frenetic activity; it is compatible with immutability.

keyTerms.definition: A series in which each member’s causal power depends, here and now, on the one before it, so the series needs a first member with underived power.
keyTerms.example: A hand moving a stick moving a stone; in this chapter, a regress of laws each borrowing explanatory power from the next.
keyTerms.origin: Scholastic *per se* (“essentially ordered”) series, contrasted with *per accidens* series; chapter 1.
keyTerms.confuseWith: Linear (per accidens) series — a temporal chain like parents and grandparents, which could in principle go back forever without contradiction.

keyTerms.definition: Features that many things can share, such as being an electron or being triangular.
keyTerms.example: Feser lists the nature of the universals mentioned in scientific laws (quark, electron) as a question science raises but philosophy must answer.
keyTerms.origin: Latin *universalia*; the medieval problem of universals goes back to Plato and Aristotle.
keyTerms.confuseWith: Collections — the universal “electron” isn’t the set of all electrons but what each has in common.

keyTerms.definition: The view that scientific theories are merely useful tools for predicting experience, not descriptions of objective reality.
keyTerms.example: Whether theories describe reality or are just predictive instruments is one of the interpretive questions Feser says science cannot settle by itself.
keyTerms.origin: Associated with Pierre Duhem and, in pragmatist form, John Dewey.
keyTerms.confuseWith: Scientism — scientism exalts science as the only knowledge; instrumentalism denies that theories give knowledge of reality at all.

keyTerms.definition: The fallacy of rejecting an argument by attacking the person who offers it rather than the argument.
keyTerms.example: “Believers only argue for God because they want him to exist.”
keyTerms.origin: Latin, “to the person.”
keyTerms.confuseWith: Fair criticism of someone’s reasoning — pointing out that a person’s argument has a false premise is not ad hominem; dismissing it because of who they are is.

keyTerms.definition: Adopted for no reason except to rescue a position from a specific difficulty.
keyTerms.example: Feser says treating the fundamental laws as a brute fact is ad hoc: its only motive is escaping arguments like the five proofs.
keyTerms.origin: Latin, “for this [purpose].”
keyTerms.confuseWith: Simply unproven — an ad hoc claim isn’t merely lacking proof; it has no independent motivation apart from the conclusion it protects.

keyTerms.definition: The methodological preference for explanations that posit fewer entities or assumptions.
keyTerms.example: Dawkins’ critic of design says a naturalistic explanation is more parsimonious; Feser replies parsimony is a standard for weighing hypotheses, not for assessing demonstrations.
keyTerms.origin: Named after William of Ockham (14th century), though he never stated the famous formula.
keyTerms.confuseWith: A proof of nonexistence — parsimony guides choice among rival explanations; it cannot refute a valid deduction from true premises.

keyTerms.definition: The power to do anything that is intrinsically possible — which excludes contradictions, since these are not really things to be done. An omnipotent being is one that has this power.
keyTerms.example: Even God cannot make a round square; so if some goods logically require permitting evils, God cannot have the goods without them.
keyTerms.origin: Latin *omnipotentia*, “all-power”; the classical understanding is Aquinas’s (*Summa Theologiae* I, q. 25).
keyTerms.confuseWith: The power to do literally anything, including contradictions — the view Mackie’s premise assumes and chapter 6 rejects.

keyTerms.definition: The absence of something that ought to be present in a thing; on the classical view evil is a privation, not a positive substance. Evil understood this way is a real lack, not an illusion.
keyTerms.example: Blindness is the privation of sight in an animal that should see; Feser treats this analysis in chapter 6 and refers back to it here.
keyTerms.origin: Latin *privatio*, “deprivation”; developed by Augustine and Aquinas from Aristotle.
keyTerms.confuseWith: Mere absence — a stone lacks sight but isn’t blind; privation is a lack of what is due to a thing’s nature.

keyTerms.definition: The argument that God may permit moral evil because a world with free creatures is good, and free creatures can misuse their freedom.
keyTerms.example: Mackie replied that God could have made free creatures who always choose good; Plantinga denied God could guarantee that; Feser grants Mackie’s point and appeals to goods like forgiveness that require actual evil.
keyTerms.origin: Classical roots in Augustine; the modern form is Alvin Plantinga’s.
keyTerms.confuseWith: Feser’s own reply — Feser relies less on free will in the abstract than on the specific virtues (mercy, courage, compassion) that presuppose evil.

keyTerms.definition: Leibniz’s thesis that a perfect God must create, and has created, the best world possible.
keyTerms.example: Feser explicitly rejects it in a footnote: God could have created nothing, or a world better in various respects.
keyTerms.origin: G. W. Leibniz, *Theodicy* (1710); satirized in Voltaire’s *Candide*.
keyTerms.confuseWith: Feser’s claim — Feser says only that God permits this world’s evils to draw goods from them, not that this world is the best possible.

keyTerms.definition: A form of argument that refutes a claim by showing that it leads to absurdity or self-contradiction.
keyTerms.example: Feser says PSR rightly understood can be established by a reductio of any attempt to deny it.
keyTerms.origin: Latin, “reduction to the absurd”; used since Zeno and Euclid.
keyTerms.confuseWith: Ridicule — a reductio shows a logical absurdity follows; it doesn’t merely make a view look silly.

keyTerms.definition: Knowable independently of experience.
keyTerms.example: The Aristotelian proof is not a priori, because its starting premise (change occurs) is known through experience — yet no future experience can overturn it.
keyTerms.origin: Latin, “from what is prior.”
keyTerms.confuseWith: Certain — a premise can be known by experience and still be certain and immune to empirical refutation, as the premise that change occurs is.

keyTerms.definition: The traditional phrase marking the completion of a proof.
keyTerms.example: Feser ends the book with it after claiming the five proofs survive every objection.
keyTerms.origin: Latin, “which was to be demonstrated,” translating Euclid’s Greek *hoper edei deixai*.
keyTerms.confuseWith: A claim that no one can dispute — Q.E.D. marks a completed demonstration, not the absence of critics.

keyTerms.definition: In Plato, goodness itself, participation in which makes things good to whatever degree they are.
keyTerms.example: Feser’s imagined anti-Platonist who says the Form of the Good is imperfectly good confuses the standard with an instance — like the “one god further” objector.
keyTerms.origin: Plato, *Republic* books 6–7 (the Sun analogy).
keyTerms.confuseWith: A very good object — the Form doesn’t *have* goodness to a high degree; it *is* goodness.

keyTerms.definition: An objection to Plato’s Forms: if large things share a Form of Largeness, then the Form and the large things share a further Form, and so on without end.
keyTerms.example: Feser says even if it succeeds, it shows there is no Form of the Good — not that the Form is imperfect.
keyTerms.origin: Plato’s *Parmenides*; named by Aristotle.
keyTerms.confuseWith: The “who made God?” regress — the Third Man concerns forms of sharing features; Feser’s point is only about what kind of conclusion an objection could establish.

keyTerms.definition: Pantheism identifies God with the world; polytheism affirms many gods.
keyTerms.example: In answering hiddenness, Feser counts pantheists and polytheists among the vast majority of humans who have affirmed some divine reality.
keyTerms.origin: Greek *pan* “all” + *theos* “god”; *polys* “many” + *theos*.
keyTerms.confuseWith: Classical theism — which holds one God distinct from the world, not identical with it and not one god among many.

keyTerms.definition: A thing’s essence is what it is; its existence is the fact that it is. The Thomistic proof argues these are really distinct in everything except God, whose essence just is existence.
keyTerms.example: Knowing what a dodo is (its essence) doesn’t tell you whether dodos exist; that’s why God can’t share an essence with Zeus and Thor.
keyTerms.origin: Latin *essentia* and *esse*; the real distinction is Aquinas’s, in *On Being and Essence* (chapter 4).
keyTerms.confuseWith: Definition vs. instance — the point isn’t just that concepts differ from things, but that in every creature what-it-is and that-it-is are distinct metaphysical principles.

keyTerms.definition: A genus is a general kind (animal); a specific difference is what marks off one species within it (rational, for human beings). Belonging to a species means being a composite of the two.
keyTerms.example: If God belonged to the genus “gods,” he would be godhood-in-general plus some distinguishing difference — and so composite.
keyTerms.origin: Aristotle’s logic of definition (Greek *genos* “kind,” *diaphora* “difference”), transmitted through Porphyry.
keyTerms.confuseWith: Biological classification — the logical genus/difference structure is more general than scientific taxonomy.

keyTerms.definition: Having parts of any kind — physical parts, or metaphysical ones like essence and existence or act and potency. A composite thing has parts; a noncomposite (simple) thing has none.
keyTerms.example: A pebble is composite even though it isn’t complex; the Neo-Platonic proof needs only composition.
keyTerms.origin: Latin *compositio*, “putting together”; central to Plotinus and the Neo-Platonic proof.
keyTerms.confuseWith: Complexity — complexity (Paley’s sense) is many parts arranged for a function; composition is having parts at all.

keyTerms.definition: Actuality is the way a thing is here and now; potentiality is a real capacity to be otherwise. Change is the actualization of a potential, and a potential can be actualized only by something already actual.
keyTerms.example: Ice is actually solid and potentially liquid; heat actualizes that potential.
keyTerms.origin: Aristotle’s *energeia* and *dynamis*; Latin *actus* and *potentia*.
keyTerms.confuseWith: Possibility — a potency is a real capacity rooted in a thing, not a mere logical possibility.

keyTerms.definition: The principle that any potential that is actualized is actualized by something already actual (in some versions: whatever comes into existence or is contingent has a cause).
keyTerms.example: Feser says this premise of the Aristotelian proof can be defended by showing that it follows from PSR.
keyTerms.origin: A central Aristotelian-Thomistic principle, defended in chapter 1.
keyTerms.confuseWith: PSR — PSR concerns explanation in general (possibly by a thing’s own nature); the principle of causality concerns what actualizes potentials.

keyTerms.definition: A contingent thing could have failed to exist and depends on something else; a necessary being cannot fail to exist and explains its own existence by its nature. “Necessary” is also used of truths that could not have been otherwise.
keyTerms.example: The fundamental laws of physics could have been different, so they are contingent; this is why Feser says only an absolutely necessary being can end a regress of explanations.
keyTerms.origin: Latin *necesse*, “unavoidable,” and *contingere*, “to happen”; the rationalist proof of chapter 5.
keyTerms.confuseWith: Very important or indispensable — “necessary being” means existing by nature, not merely being needed by other things.

keyTerms.definition: Something whose existence is explained by its own nature, so that it can impart explanatory power without deriving it. For Feser, only what is purely actual, simple, with essence identical to existence, and necessary qualifies.
keyTerms.example: In the brute-fact reply, the regress of laws must end in a self-explanatory being, not in an unexplained law.
