explain.keyAnalogy: **The metal detector.** Feser’s best single image for this half-chapter: a metal detector outperforms every other method at finding metal, but even a perfect record wouldn’t make it likely that only metal exists. Use it to show that science’s success proves its power within its domain, not that its domain is everything. Then extend it: demanding the “predictions” of metaphysics is like demanding the metal-detecting record of a spatula; and being told “your arguments aren’t scientific” is like being told your sandwich isn’t real because the detector didn’t beep. Once someone sees that science is a superb, *targeted* instrument, scientism loses its grip — and with it the reason for dismissing the proofs without examining them. For the “one god further” objection, pair it with the second-best analogy: confusing God with Zeus is like confusing triangularity with a triangle drawn on a chalkboard.

persuade.coreInsight:
The idea that makes this chapter click is that **most popular objections aren’t really objections to the five proofs at all** — they are objections to something else. Scientism objects to non-scientific knowledge as such, but refutes itself in doing so. The complex-designer and one-god-further objections object to a God who is one more complex being in the universe, which is exactly what the proofs deny. The motive and disagreement objections object to the arguers, not the arguments. Once a listener sees that the target has been missed, the conversation can turn to the only question that matters: is some premise of a proof false, or some step invalid?

The usual reason this fails to click is that scientism is invisible to people who hold it. It doesn’t feel like a philosophical position; it feels like common sense, backed by every smartphone and vaccine. So don’t attack science — praise it. Then ask, gently, how science could establish that it is the only route to truth. The shift from “science has succeeded” to “only science tells us anything” is where the listener has to notice a step they never knew they took.

On suffering, the core insight is different: the intellectual objection and the lived experience are two different things. Feser answers the first with a modest *defense*, not a claim to know God’s reasons. If you remember that you don’t know why a particular tragedy happened — and say so — you will be both more honest and more persuasive than someone who rushes to explain it.

audiences.startingPoint: Science is the best, perhaps only, reliable path to knowledge; religion makes untestable claims; appeals to God are placeholders for ignorance.
audiences.approach: Start by sincerely affirming the achievements of science — Feser does too. Then separate science from scientism. Walk through the airplane-engineer example and the metal detector, and ask what experiment could show that only experiments yield knowledge. Point out that the proofs don’t compete with any scientific theory; they start from what any scientific theory presupposes (that things change, have parts, exist contingently). Invite them to evaluate a proof by the standards appropriate to a deduction: is a premise false, or does the conclusion not follow?
audiences.openingQuestion: What’s the scientific experiment that shows science is the only way to know things?
audiences.avoid: Don’t disparage science, cite scientific “gaps,” or imply that God competes with physics as an explanation. That confirms their suspicion that you’re offering a god of the gaps.

audiences.startingPoint: Has heard “Who designed the designer?” and “one god further” and regards them as knockout punches; thinks theists are rationalizing.
audiences.approach: Stay cheerful and precise. Concede what’s true: a complex designer *would* need a cause — which is why the proofs conclude to something with no parts. Explain that classical theism’s God isn’t a member of the category “gods,” using the triangularity analogy or the author-and-characters image. On motives, grant freely that you’d like God to exist, then ask which premise that makes false. Keep bringing the discussion back to a specific premise.
audiences.openingQuestion: Which of the five proofs have you looked at — and which premise do you think fails?
audiences.avoid: Don’t get pulled into swapping insults about motives, and don’t defend Paley-style design arguments as if they were the proofs at issue.

audiences.startingPoint: A real loss or ongoing pain makes God seem absent or cruel; arguments feel like a dismissal of their experience.
audiences.approach: Listen first and longest. Acknowledge the evil as evil. Admit honestly that you don’t know why this happened — Feser doesn’t claim to either. If and when they want to think it through, share gently: that the reasons for believing in God don’t depend on explaining this event; that some of the deepest goods (mercy, courage, compassion) exist only where there is suffering; that if God is real, this is not the end of the story. Let them set the pace; return to the conversation later rather than finishing it now.
audiences.openingQuestion: Would it help to talk about it, or would you rather I just be here?
audiences.avoid: Never say “everything happens for a reason” or suggest that their suffering is secretly good or deserved. Don’t lead with Mackie or Rowe. Don’t treat their pain as a debating move.

audiences.startingPoint: Genuinely unsure; troubled that if God existed he would be more obvious; notes that smart people disagree.
audiences.approach: Take their honesty seriously and don’t accuse them of bad faith. Explain that hiddenness assumes God would make himself obvious to everyone and that he hasn’t — then note that most people in history have found belief in God natural, and that finite minds and free attention make error possible for anyone. Explain that controversy doesn’t equal failure: every major philosophical argument has critics. Offer to go through one proof slowly, as a demonstration to be checked, not a sales pitch.
audiences.openingQuestion: If there were a good argument for God, what would you want it to look like?
audiences.avoid: Don’t overstate certainty in a way that ignores their real questions, and don’t imply that doubt itself is a moral failing.

audiences.startingPoint: Worries that the purely actual, simple First Cause is a cold abstraction, not the God of prayer and scripture.
audiences.approach: Use Feser’s two points: if the proofs work, atheism is false regardless; and the God of the proofs is the same God believers worship, known by a different route — the Catholic tradition teaches some truths about God are known by both reason and revelation, others only by revelation. Use the ball-and-stick atoms analogy: they already believe in the God the philosophers describe, just without the technical vocabulary.
audiences.openingQuestion: When you pray to God as the Creator who is all-powerful and all-good, what do you think you’re affirming about him?
audiences.avoid: Don’t make philosophy sound like a replacement for faith or suggest that ordinary believers’ faith is defective because it isn’t technical.

audiences.startingPoint: Familiar with naturalized metaphysics (Ladyman and Ross), Rowe’s evidential argument, and Schellenberg; skeptical of a priori metaphysics.
audiences.approach: Engage at full strength. Press the self-refutation of the “science or conceptual analysis” dichotomy and the problem that logic and mathematics pose for it. On Rowe, show that the argument’s force depends on the absence of independent evidence for theism, and that Rowe concedes a hidden good is possible. On Schellenberg, separate the two assumptions. Emphasize that the proofs are presented as deductions whose premises can be attacked — invite them to do so.
audiences.openingQuestion: Is the claim that all legitimate inquiry is either empirical science or conceptual analysis itself empirical, or conceptual?
audiences.avoid: Don’t pretend Feser’s positions are uncontroversial in the academy or wave away serious contemporary work; acknowledge the debate while pressing the arguments.

dialogue.speaker: Skeptic
dialogue.line: Honestly, I don’t see the point of these proofs. Science is how we know things, and no scientific theory needs God.

dialogue.speaker: You
dialogue.line: I agree science is incredibly successful. Can I ask a question about the first part, though — that science is how we know things. Is that the *only* way?

dialogue.speaker: Skeptic
dialogue.line: It’s the only reliable way. Everything else is opinion.

dialogue.speaker: You
dialogue.line: Then how do we know that? Is there an experiment that shows science is the only reliable way to know things?

dialogue.speaker: Skeptic
dialogue.line: Well, no, but look at the track record. Physics predicts things to ten decimal places. Nothing else comes close.

dialogue.speaker: You
dialogue.line: Totally. But compare a metal detector. It finds coins better than any other method. Would that make it likely that only metal exists?

dialogue.speaker: Skeptic
dialogue.line: No, but a metal detector is only looking for one kind of thing. Science looks at everything.

dialogue.speaker: You
dialogue.line: That’s actually the question, isn’t it? Physics works by describing things mathematically. Colors as experienced, meanings, purposes — it leaves those out on purpose. It’s like airline engineers treating passengers as average weights: brilliant for loading the plane, but no one concludes passengers have no taste in food.

dialogue.speaker: Skeptic
dialogue.line: Okay, so science has limits. That still doesn’t get you to God. Maybe the laws of physics are just the bottom level. They exist, full stop.

dialogue.speaker: You
dialogue.line: Then here’s the worry: if the deepest law explains nothing about why it holds, how does anything built on it get explained? It’s like resting a shelf on brackets and then letting go of the brackets in midair. The proofs argue the chain has to end in something that doesn’t borrow its existence — something whose very nature is to exist.

dialogue.speaker: Skeptic
dialogue.line: But then who made God? A mind that could design a universe would be more complex than the universe.

dialogue.speaker: You
dialogue.line: I agree a complex cause would need a cause. That’s exactly why the proofs conclude the first cause has no parts at all — it’s absolutely simple. They’re not design arguments about eyes and flagella; they’d work starting from a pebble.

dialogue.speaker: Skeptic
dialogue.line: Fine, but you already reject Zeus and Thor. I just go one god further.

dialogue.speaker: You
dialogue.line: Zeus is a being inside the world — body, parents, moods, a beginning. The God of the proofs isn’t one more being in that lineup; he’s being itself, the source of anything existing at all. It’s a bit like saying, ‘You admit every drawn triangle is imperfect — I just go one step further and say triangularity itself is crooked.’ It isn’t the same kind of claim.

dialogue.speaker: Skeptic
dialogue.line: Here’s what really bothers me. My sister spent two years in pain before she died. If there’s a good God, why?

dialogue.speaker: You
dialogue.line: I’m really sorry. That’s awful, and I won’t pretend I know why it happened. Can I ask — do you want to talk about her, or about the question?

dialogue.speaker: Skeptic
dialogue.line: The question, I guess. I’ve thought about it a lot.

dialogue.speaker: You
dialogue.line: Then honestly: the argument I find strongest isn’t that I can explain it. It’s that some of the best things in people — courage, mercy, compassion like you probably showed her — can only exist where there’s suffering. And if we have good independent reasons to think God exists and is good, then my not seeing the reason doesn’t mean there isn’t one. It’s a bit like a child who can’t see why something hard was worth it until much later — except the distance is far greater.

dialogue.speaker: Skeptic
dialogue.line: That sounds like you’ve made your belief impossible to disprove.

dialogue.speaker: You
dialogue.line: It can be disproved — by showing one of the proofs has a false premise or a bad step. What it can’t be disproved by is my inability to see God’s reasons. If you want to take a shot at one of the premises, I’m game.

dialogue.speaker: Skeptic
dialogue.line: And if God wanted a relationship with me, wouldn’t he make it obvious? Plenty of smart people don’t believe.

dialogue.speaker: You
dialogue.line: Most people in history *have* found God pretty obvious — that’s actually a complaint atheists make about ordinary believers. And smart people disagree about every serious philosophical argument; that’s not the same as the argument failing. Our minds are finite and we choose where to look. Which is why I’d rather look at one proof carefully with you than trade slogans.

dialogue.speaker: Skeptic
dialogue.line: Aren’t these proofs just rationalizations of what you already wanted to believe?

dialogue.speaker: You
dialogue.line: Maybe I want God to exist — Thomas Nagel admitted he wants God not to. Either way, that doesn’t make a premise false. So: which premise do you think fails?

socratic: Can the claim “only science gives knowledge” be tested by a scientific experiment? If not, how do you know it?
What does science have to assume before it can begin — that there is a real world, that it is orderly, that our minds can grasp it? Could science prove those without assuming them?
If a method is designed to measure only quantities, what would you expect it to say about qualities, meanings, or purposes?
Does a metal detector’s perfect success rate make it likely that only metal exists? What’s different about the argument from science’s success?
If law A is explained by law B, and law B by nothing at all, does law A really explain anything?
The proofs conclude that the first cause has no parts. Does the question “who caused the cause?” still apply to something with no parts and no potential to be caused?
Is triangularity one more triangle — only bigger or better drawn? Is the source of all being one more being?
Can you have forgiveness where no one has done wrong, or courage where there is no danger?
If you had strong independent reason to trust someone’s goodness and wisdom, should “I can’t see why they did this” lead you to conclude “they had no reason”?
If most people in history have believed in some divine reality, in what sense is God hidden from most people?
Does knowing why someone gives an argument tell you whether its premises are true?
Name a major philosophical argument — for materialism, against free will — that everyone who hears it accepts. Does its having critics mean it fails?

traps.trap: Attacking science instead of scientism — sounding anti-scientific, mocking scientists, or pointing to what science “can’t explain yet.”
traps.fix: Praise science wholeheartedly and locate the problem precisely: the philosophical claim that science is the only source of knowledge. Never argue from current scientific gaps; the proofs start from what any science presupposes.

traps.trap: Answering suffering with a lecture — reaching for Mackie, Rowe, and greater goods when someone is grieving.
traps.fix: Listen first, acknowledge the evil as evil, and admit you don’t know why it happened. Feser’s argument is a defense, not an explanation of any particular tragedy. Offer the reasoning only when it’s wanted, and gently.

traps.trap: Saying “everything happens for a reason” or implying suffering is secretly good.
traps.fix: Feser holds evil is a real privation. The claim is that God can draw greater goods from evil, not that evil is good. Say “I believe it isn’t the last word,” not “it was meant to be.”

traps.trap: Defending Paley or Intelligent Design when someone raises “who designed the designer.”
traps.fix: Point out that the five proofs aren’t design arguments: they don’t appeal to complexity or probability, and they conclude to an absolutely simple cause precisely because complex things need causes.

traps.trap: Answering “one god further” only by saying there’s more evidence for your God.
traps.fix: That’s Feser’s first point, but lead with the category distinction: God is not a member of the class “gods” but being itself. Use the triangle-vs.-triangularity or author-vs.-character analogy.

traps.trap: Returning the motive charge with interest — accusing atheists of wanting to avoid moral accountability.
traps.fix: Feser cites Nagel only to show the charge cuts both ways, and insists not all atheists are dishonest. Make the symmetric point and then drop motives entirely: which premise fails?

traps.trap: Overclaiming — presenting the proofs as so obvious that anyone who rejects them is stupid or dishonest.
traps.fix: Feser grants that a demonstration may require serious work and that fair, informed people may not see its force. Controversy isn’t failure, but it isn’t stupidity either. Invite scrutiny premise by premise.

traps.trap: Getting lost in a dozen objections at once instead of diagnosing the common move.
traps.fix: Sort the objection: does it refute itself, attack a caricature of God, or apply the wrong standard (probability, motive, universal assent)? Name the move in a sentence, then return to a specific premise.

connections.note: Part A handles the technical objections to the cosmological argument (“what caused God?”, Hume’s and quantum mechanics’ challenges to causation, composition, god of the gaps, Krauss’ universe from “nothing”). Part B picks up where the god-of-the-gaps discussion left off, digging out the scientism behind it, and relies on Part A’s results — e.g., Gerson’s point that “maybe there’s no explanation” can’t answer an offered explanation.

The hierarchical (per se) causal series of the Aristotelian proof returns in the brute-fact reply: a regress of laws, like a regress of instrumental causes, needs a first member with underived power. The closing account of demonstration uses the Aristotelian proof as its example (change can’t be refuted by any future experience, since every experience is a change).

The Neo-Platonic proof’s starting point — that things are composite — is contrasted with Paley-style “complexity”: any composite thing, even a pebble or a drop of water, will do. Its conclusion, an absolutely simple One, is why the complex-designer objection misses.

The Augustinian proof’s defense of the necessity and objectivity of logical and mathematical truths is what breaks Hume’s Fork and the “science or conceptual analysis” dichotomy; natural theology’s truths are placed alongside them.
The Thomistic proof’s God, whose essence is his existence, is the God who is not “a being” among others but subsistent being itself — the key to answering “one god further.”

The principle of sufficient reason defended in the rationalist proof is invoked repeatedly: against the claim that ultimate explanation is unavailable, against treating the laws as brute facts, and in the account of how the premises of a demonstration are defended.

Divine simplicity, immutability, immateriality, and necessity underwrite the contrast between the God of classical theism and the limited pagan gods, and between a self-explanatory ground and a brute fact.

Feser’s replies to Mackie and Rowe build directly on chapter 6’s account of omnipotence (no power to do contradictions), goodness, evil as privation, whether God must create the best world, and God’s love; the hiddenness reply reuses the same greater-good reasoning.

The introduction promised that chapter 7 would show the most common objections to be feeble and overrated, and that the real debate is not atheism vs. theism but among theists of different stripes. Part B makes good on both: the popular objections are dismantled one by one, and the reply to “the philosophers’ God isn’t the believer’s God” repeats the point that the serious remaining debate is among theists.

This module supplies the diagnostic toolkit for the capstone: sort any objection by whether it refutes itself, attacks a caricature, or applies the wrong standard, then return to a specific premise. It also contains the book’s concluding account of what it means for the five proofs to be demonstrations.

quiz.q: How does Feser define scientism?
options: The practice of using controlled experiments to test hypotheses
The view that science and religion address separate, non-overlapping questions
The view that science alone gives genuine knowledge, so legitimate philosophy is only what is implicit in science
The view that scientific theories are merely useful tools for prediction
quiz.explanation: Scientism is a philosophical thesis about the scope of knowledge, not the practice of science itself. The last option describes instrumentalism, one of the interpretive questions Feser says philosophy must settle.

quiz.q: Why, according to Feser, is scientism self-refuting when taken strictly?
options: Because the claim that only science yields knowledge cannot itself be established by scientific method, and science rests on presuppositions only an extrascientific standpoint could justify
Because scientific theories are constantly revised and so never yield certainty
Because scientists disagree among themselves about fundamental physics
Because science cannot yet explain the origin of the universe
quiz.explanation: The self-refutation lies in the thesis’s own status: it is a philosophical claim that science cannot establish. Revisability and current gaps are not Feser’s argument; he explicitly avoids god-of-the-gaps reasoning.

quiz.q: What goes wrong if the defender of scientism responds by counting philosophy as part of “science”?
options: Science would lose its predictive power
Philosophy would have to adopt mathematical methods
Nothing — this is Feser’s preferred resolution
The thesis becomes trivial, and it can no longer exclude natural theology, which Aristotle and Aquinas regarded as a science
quiz.explanation: This is the second horn of the dilemma. A definition of science broad enough to include philosophy has no non-arbitrary way of excluding natural theology, so scientism can no longer serve its purpose of dismissing it unheard.

quiz.q: The example of engineers treating airline passengers as average weights is meant to show that…
options: physics is less reliable than engineering
a feature’s absence from an abstract description may result from the method’s design rather than from the feature’s nonexistence
human beings are ultimately reducible to physical quantities
averages never correspond to any actual individual
quiz.explanation: The engineers’ data say nothing about meal preferences because the method looks only at weight. Likewise physics leaves out qualities, meanings, and purposes by design. The last option is a detail of the example, not its point.

quiz.q: What point does Feser take from Bertrand Russell about physics?
options: Physics will eventually explain consciousness
Physics gives only the abstract mathematical structure of events, not the intrinsic nature of what has that structure
Physics proves that the universe had a beginning
Physics shows that causation is merely constant conjunction
quiz.explanation: Russell, no friend of theism, stressed physics’ abstractness. Feser adds that since structure must be the structure of something, physics itself implies there is more to reality than it describes.

quiz.q: Why does the Humean view of laws of nature give no support to the idea that science provides the ultimate explanation of the world?
options: Because Hume believed laws were decrees of God
Because on this view laws are abstract objects outside the physical world
Because on this view laws describe the essences of things, which must already exist
Because on this view laws only summarize regularities, telling us that a pattern holds but not why
quiz.explanation: Humean laws redescribe rather than explain. The other options describe the Cartesian-Newtonian, Platonic, and Aristotelian views, each of which fails for a different reason.

quiz.q: Feser compares Rosenberg’s argument from the success of science to which argument?
options: Metal detectors find metal better than any other method, so metallic objects are probably all that is real
Telescopes see farther than eyes, so eyes are unreliable
Maps are useful, so the territory must be flat
Medicine cures diseases, so all illness is physical
quiz.explanation: The metal-detector parody has exactly the same form: from unmatched success at detecting one kind of thing to the claim that probably nothing else exists.

quiz.q: Rosenberg says critics of scientism happily trust their cardiologists but cry “scientism” when their metaphysics is scrutinized. What is Feser’s reply?
options: Critics of scientism should stop relying on cardiologists
Cardiology is not really a science
Trusting a method within its domain doesn’t commit you to its having no limits — like trusting metal detectors without thinking they alone detect physical things
Metaphysics can also be tested by cardiology
quiz.explanation: The charge of inconsistency assumes that trusting science anywhere requires trusting it as the sole source of knowledge. Insisting that science, unlike metal detectors, covers all of reality would beg the question.

quiz.q: Feser’s analogy of the student who takes only easy courses and boasts of his GPA is aimed at which claim?
options: That philosophy has made no progress since Aristotle
That natural theology is a kind of science
That scientific theories are revisable
That even if science can’t answer everything, it answers everything worth knowing, as shown by its consensus and technology
quiz.explanation: If only predictable, consensus-yielding questions count as scientific, science’s success is guaranteed trivially and says nothing about the value of the questions it excludes. The claim is also itself philosophical.

quiz.q: Why does Feser say the claim that any non-scientific inquiry is mere “conceptual analysis” refutes itself?
options: Because conceptual analysis always yields false results
Because the claim itself is neither a conceptual truth nor something natural science could support — like Hume’s Fork
Because Ladyman and Ross are not scientists
Because neuroscience has disproved conceptual analysis
quiz.explanation: The dichotomy falls between its own tines. Feser adds that appealing to neuroscience would beg the question, since whether such sciences are our only source of knowledge about cognition is what is at issue.

quiz.q: What role do the truths of logic and mathematics play in Feser’s critique of scientism?
options: They show that all knowledge is ultimately empirical
They prove that God exists directly
They are knowledge that fits neither tine of Hume’s Fork, being necessary (unlike science) and objective (unlike mere conceptual analysis)
They show that philosophy is just a branch of mathematics
quiz.explanation: Logic and mathematics are counterexamples to the science-or-conceptual-analysis dichotomy, and Feser places the conclusions of natural theology in the same category.

quiz.q: Which thinkers does Feser say essentially held that the fundamental laws of nature are an unexplained brute fact?
options: J. L. Mackie and Bertrand Russell
Aristotle and Aquinas
Descartes and Newton
Plato and Plotinus
quiz.explanation: Feser cites Mackie’s *The Miracle of Theism* and Russell’s debate with Copleston. Descartes and Newton held a theological view of laws; Aristotle and Aquinas grounded laws in natures.

quiz.q: What is the point of the image of a book on a shelf held up by brackets that are then let go in midair?
options: If the fundamental laws are unexplained, the higher-level laws that depend on them cannot really explain anything either
Physical objects need support to stay in place
The universe had a beginning in time
Laws of nature change over time
quiz.explanation: A regress of laws is like a hierarchical causal series: without a self-explanatory first member, borrowed explanatory power has no source. That is the third problem with the brute-fact view.

quiz.q: What does Feser call the most important problem with the objection that a designer would be more complex than the universe?
options: Dawkins misread Paley
Complexity is subjective
The five proofs agree that a complex cause would need a cause, which is exactly why they conclude the first cause is absolutely simple
Probabilistic reasoning is always unreliable
quiz.explanation: Feser gives three replies (no appeal to complexity, no appeal to probability, and this one), and calls this the most important: the objection presupposes a composite God that the proofs explicitly rule out.

quiz.q: Which starting point would serve the Neo-Platonic proof but would never be used by Paley or an Intelligent Design theorist?
options: The human eye
A pebble or a drop of water
The bacterial flagellum
A pocket watch
quiz.explanation: The Neo-Platonic proof needs only something composite; it doesn’t care how many parts or how precisely arranged. Paley’s argument needs intricate, function-serving complexity.

quiz.q: According to Feser, the deeper flaw in the “one god further” objection is that it…
options: ignores the historical influence of polytheism
overlooks that some pagans were monotheists
fails to count all the gods correctly
commits a category mistake by treating the God of classical theism as one member of a class of beings called “gods”
quiz.explanation: The first reply is that there are arguments for God and none for Zeus; the deeper one is that God is in no genus, shares no essence with other gods, and is being itself rather than a being.

quiz.q: In Feser’s anti-Euclidean analogy, if physical space turned out to be non-Euclidean, what would follow about Euclidean triangles?
options: They would turn out to have imperfectly straight sides
They would be identical to non-Euclidean triangles
They would simply not be instantiated, rather than being imperfectly straight
They would become merely conceptual
quiz.explanation: The claim that Euclidean triangles have crooked sides doesn’t even make sense. Likewise, if atheism were true, it wouldn’t be because God is one more nonexistent god — the objection misdescribes what is being denied.

quiz.q: According to the Catholic teaching Feser cites, which truth about God is knowable only through divine revelation?
options: That God is omnipotent
That God is omniscient
That God is the cause of the world
That God is a Trinity
quiz.explanation: Omnipotence and omniscience can be known both by reason and by revelation; the Trinity only by revelation. It is the same God known by different routes.

quiz.q: What is the difference between a defense and a theodicy?
options: A defense is religious; a theodicy is philosophical
A defense shows that evil is logically compatible with God; a theodicy tries to say why God actually permits the evils that exist
A defense addresses moral evil; a theodicy addresses natural evil
There is no difference; the terms are synonyms
quiz.explanation: Feser offers a defense, which suffices to rebut the objection. He notes older Thomistic works used “theodicy” to mean natural theology in general, but not that the terms are synonyms in the modern sense.

quiz.q: How does Feser answer Mackie’s claim that God could have created free creatures who always freely choose good?
options: He grants that such a world is possible but argues it couldn’t contain goods like forgiveness, mercy, courage, and compassion, which presuppose actual evil
He denies it, following Plantinga, on the grounds that any free creatures would sometimes sin
He argues that free will is an illusion
He argues that this is the best of all possible worlds
quiz.explanation: Feser explicitly says the theist need not take Plantinga’s route, and in a footnote he rejects Leibniz’s best-possible-world claim. His point is that certain moral goods require evil.

quiz.q: Why does Feser think Rowe’s evidential argument poses no challenge to the book’s proofs?
options: Because animals do not really suffer
Because Rowe’s example is fictional
Because suffering is always a punishment for sin
Because believing there is no greater good is rational only if we lack independent reason to think a good God exists, and the proofs supply such reason
quiz.explanation: Rowe concedes a hidden greater good is possible. Given independent proof of an omnipotent, omniscient, perfectly good God, we have reason to think such a good is actual. To challenge the proofs, the argument would first have to refute them.

quiz.q: Why is Schellenberg’s hiddenness argument a nonstarter against Aristotle’s theism?
options: Because Aristotle’s Unmoved Mover contemplates itself and takes no notice of us, so it doesn’t seek a personal relationship
Because Aristotle believed God was obvious to everyone
Because Aristotle denied that God exists
Because Aristotle held that humans lack free will
quiz.explanation: The argument assumes God intends a personal relationship with us. A theism without that assumption is untouched, so the argument fails as a completely general case for atheism — though Feser himself holds that God does seek such a relationship.

quiz.q: What does Feser use Thomas Nagel’s admission that he hopes there is no God to show?
options: That all atheists are intellectually dishonest
That the charge of motivated reasoning can be made against critics of theism too, so motives settle nothing
That Nagel secretly believes in God
That scientism is a religious belief
quiz.explanation: Feser explicitly says not all atheists are dishonest. The point is symmetry: since bias can run either way, only examining the arguments can decide.

quiz.q: Why can’t the Aristotelian proof’s premise that change occurs be overturned by future empirical inquiry?
options: Because it is known a priori, independently of experience
Because physics has confirmed it
Because any possible future experience would itself be an instance of change
Because Aristotle defined change that way
quiz.explanation: The premise is empirical in a sense (so the proof isn’t a priori), but it can’t be empirically refuted: we might show some particular change unreal, never that all change is. This is part of what makes a demonstration more secure than a scientific inference.

quiz.q: In the reconstructed case against scientism, which move secures the claim that physics itself implies there is more to reality than physics describes?
options: The point that a structure cannot exist without something that has the structure, while physics gives only structure
The point that physics has not yet reached a final theory
The point that scientists disagree about quantum mechanics
The point that physics cannot make predictions about human behavior
quiz.explanation: Steps 10–11: Russell showed physics gives only abstract structure; since structure must be the structure of something, physics points beyond itself. The other options are gap-style or irrelevant considerations Feser doesn’t use.

quiz.q: A friend says: “Neuroscience shows that any inquiry that isn’t natural science is just conceptual analysis.” What would Feser reply?
options: Neuroscience is not a real science
The appeal begs the question, since whether such sciences are our only source of knowledge about cognition is exactly what is disputed
Neuroscience actually supports Aristotelianism
Conceptual analysis is the best form of philosophy
quiz.explanation: Feser’s footnote: besides the missing evidence, neuroscience could show this only if it were our sole source of knowledge about the mind — the very point at issue.

quiz.q: Which distinction does the “one god further” objection ignore?
options: Defense vs. theodicy
Structure vs. intrinsic nature
A being among beings vs. subsistent being itself
Linear vs. hierarchical causal series
quiz.explanation: The objection treats God as one member of the class “gods.” Classical theism’s God is not a being among others but being itself, the source of all being — so rejecting him isn’t like rejecting Zeus.

quiz.q: Which distinction does the “designer would be more complex than the universe” objection ignore?
options: Science vs. scientism
Logical vs. evidential problem of evil
Crude understanding vs. a different object of belief
Strict demonstration to a simple cause vs. probabilistic design argument from complexity
quiz.explanation: The objection is built for Paley-style arguments. The five proofs aren’t probabilistic, don’t rely on complexity, and conclude to an absolutely simple cause.

quiz.q: What does Feser mean when he calls the brute-fact view of the fundamental laws “ad hoc”?
options: It has no motivation except avoiding arguments like the five proofs
It was invented by Hume
It depends on quantum mechanics
It is a claim about particular cases only
quiz.explanation: An independent motive would exist if the Humean or quantum objections to PSR succeeded, but they don’t — leaving only the desire to escape the theistic conclusion.

quiz.q: Whose observation does Feser invoke to say that an argument offering an explanation cannot be answered by “maybe there’s no explanation”?
options: Anthony Kenny
Lloyd Gerson
John Hick
David Albert
quiz.explanation: Gerson’s point (discussed in Part A) is that since the argument gives an explanation, the critic must show what is wrong with it rather than pretend it doesn’t exist.

quiz.q: A skeptic asks, “What technology has theology ever produced?” Which analogy of Feser’s best fits the reply?
options: The shelf held up by brackets
The child who doesn’t understand homework
Demanding the metal-detecting achievements of gardening, cooking, and painting
The anti-Euclidean and triangularity
quiz.explanation: The demand assumes that success at prediction and technology is the only mark of knowledge — like judging spades and spatulas by how well they detect metal.

quiz.q: Why does the Platonic view of laws of nature fail to supply an ultimate explanation?
options: Because Platonic laws are identical to God’s will
Because Platonic laws are just summaries of regularities
Because Platonic laws depend on the natures of physical things
Because we would still need to explain why a physical world participates in these laws at all, and in these rather than others
quiz.explanation: The other options describe the Cartesian-Newtonian, Humean, and Aristotelian views. On the Platonic view, something beyond the laws must account for the world’s participating in them.

quiz.q: Why doesn’t Feser need Plantinga’s claim that God might not be able to create free creatures who never sin?
options: Because even granting Mackie such a world is possible, it couldn’t contain goods like forgiveness, mercy, courage, and compassion that presuppose evil
Because Feser denies human free will
Because Plantinga’s claim was refuted by Mackie
Because Feser holds that evil is an illusion
quiz.explanation: Feser concedes Mackie’s point for the sake of argument and relocates the issue: certain moral goods exist only in a world where evil actually occurs.

quiz.q: Why is it strategically significant that Feser grants Mackie that God could have made a world with free will, morally significant choices, and no evil?
options: It shows Feser thinks the problem of evil is unanswerable
It shows his reply doesn’t depend on a contested claim and rests instead on goods that logically require evil
It shows he agrees with Leibniz that this is the best world
It shows that free will is irrelevant to morality
quiz.explanation: By granting the opponent’s strongest claim, Feser makes his defense independent of the Plantinga debate. He explicitly rejects the Leibnizian best-world thesis.

quiz.q: Someone says, “A loving parent would never let a child suffer, so a loving God wouldn’t either.” Which of Feser’s points most directly applies?
options: God is not a person at all
Suffering is always deserved punishment
A good parent sometimes permits unpleasantness, like homework, because removing it would remove goods that depend on it
Children cannot really suffer
quiz.explanation: Feser’s homework example shows that goodness doesn’t require eliminating every evil one can, since some goods presuppose those evils.

quiz.q: Why, according to Feser, should we expect not to know God’s reasons for many particular evils?
options: Because God has no reasons
Because evil is unreal
Because reasons are always private
Because an endless afterlife could hold outweighing goods that we understand no better than a small child understands adulthood
quiz.explanation: God knows infinitely more than a parent, and the afterlife differs from this life more than adulthood differs from childhood — so our incomprehension is predictable.

quiz.q: What kernel of truth does Feser find in Hick’s idea of epistemic distance?
options: God gives finite, free minds a long leash to err in what they think, just as in what they do
The universe is equally interpretable in theistic and atheistic ways
Belief in God is incompatible with free choice
Most people are atheists
quiz.explanation: Feser rejects Hick’s “religious ambiguity” but grants that finitude and free will make intellectual error — including denying God — possible and unsurprising.

quiz.q: What evidence does Feser give that Hick overstates how much a free choice about relating to God depends on doubt?
options: Surveys of modern believers
Believers throughout history have done great evils without doubting God’s existence
Aristotle’s Unmoved Mover ignores us
Children believe in God naturally
quiz.explanation: The history of ancient Israel, the Church, and Islam shows people freely rejecting God’s will without concluding atheism might be true.

quiz.q: A skeptic says, “Most people’s reasons for believing in God are weak, so God really is hidden from them.” What would Feser reply?
options: Most people’s reasons are actually strong philosophical proofs
Belief without reasons is always irrational
A layman’s weak grasp of the evidence for science doesn’t make scientific truths hidden from him, and the same holds for belief in God
Hiddenness is irrelevant to theism
quiz.explanation: Feser’s atoms analogy: nonexperts can have genuine, if unsophisticated and error-mixed, knowledge — often a simplified approximation of the real arguments.

quiz.q: What does Hilary Putnam’s remark, quoted in Feser’s footnote, contribute to the reply to “it can’t be a proof if people disagree”?
options: It shows that Putnam was a theist
It shows that analytic philosophy has refuted natural theology
It shows that proofs must be mathematical
It shows that by the standard of convincing every rational person, the philosophical arguments of Frege, Russell, Quine, and others would fail too
quiz.explanation: Putnam exposes the double standard: a test that no major philosophical argument passes is being applied only to arguments for God.

quiz.q: In what two respects does Feser say a demonstration is more secure than a scientific inference?
options: It is a strict deduction rather than a probabilistic or best-explanation inference, and its premises can’t be overturned by future empirical inquiry
It is shorter, and it uses mathematics
It is endorsed by more experts, and it is older
It relies on revelation, and it avoids premises from experience
quiz.explanation: These are the two points Feser gives. Demonstrations don’t rely on revelation, and the Aristotelian proof does use a premise from experience.

quiz.q: Which statement about the premise “change occurs” in the Aristotelian proof matches Feser’s view?
options: It is known a priori, so it is certain
It is known from experience, yet no future experience could overturn it, since any such experience would itself be a change
It is a hypothesis that physics might one day refute
It is true only of living things
quiz.explanation: The premise is empirical in a sense (so the proof isn’t a priori), but it can’t be empirically refuted: we can doubt particular changes, never change as such.

quiz.q: What is Feser’s first reply to the objection that the God of philosophical theism isn’t the God ordinary believers worship?
options: Ordinary believers are simply mistaken
The Bible teaches divine simplicity explicitly
Even if true, it would be irrelevant, since if the proofs work atheism is false and the remaining debate is among theists
Philosophical theism is a separate religion
quiz.explanation: His second reply is that the claim is false anyway — some religions identify the two and ordinary believers hold the same God in a less sophisticated way.

quiz.q: A student says, “Physics describes the world as particles and fields, so purposes and meanings aren’t real.” Which of Feser’s points applies most directly?
options: Physics is unreliable
Purposes can be measured by future physics
Meanings are merely conceptual
Physics abstracts from whatever can’t be modeled mathematically, so their absence from its description is guaranteed by method, not discovered
quiz.explanation: The airplane-engineer point: omitting a feature by method is not evidence that the feature doesn’t exist.

shortAnswer.q: Explain the dilemma Feser poses for scientism.
shortAnswer.model: Scientism is either self-refuting or trivial. Taken narrowly, the claim that only science gives knowledge is not itself scientifically established, and science rests on presuppositions (a mind-independent, orderly world knowable by our faculties) it cannot justify without circularity; it also needs philosophy to interpret its results. So the thesis undercuts itself. Taken broadly — counting philosophy as “science” — it becomes vacuous and can no longer exclude natural theology, which Aristotle and Aquinas regarded as a science more certain than physics. Either way it cannot justify dismissing natural theology unheard.
rubric: States both horns: self-refuting vs. trivial
Explains why the thesis isn’t scientifically established
Mentions science’s philosophical presuppositions and/or need for interpretation
Explains why the broad version lets natural theology in and defeats scientism’s purpose

shortAnswer.q: Why can’t physics give a complete description even of physical reality?
shortAnswer.model: Physics deliberately restricts itself to what can be described mathematically, and so predicted and controlled. Everything qualitative — colors as experienced, sounds, thoughts, purposes, meanings — falls through its net by design, as the airplane engineers’ weight calculations leave out passengers’ tastes. Its silence about such features is not evidence that they don’t exist. Moreover, as Russell stressed, physics gives only abstract structure, not the intrinsic nature of what has the structure; since there can’t be structure without something structured, physics itself implies there is more to reality than it describes.
rubric: Methodological restriction to the quantitative
The engineers analogy or equivalent point that silence isn’t denial
Russell’s structure vs. intrinsic nature point
The inference that structure implies something beyond structure

shortAnswer.q: Reconstruct the argument from the success of science and explain why Feser thinks it fails.
shortAnswer.model: Premise: science’s predictive power and technological applications are unmatched. Conclusion: what science reveals is probably all that is real. It fails because success at capturing one aspect of reality doesn’t show there are no others — just as metal detectors’ unmatched success at finding metal doesn’t make it probable that only metal exists. Physics succeeds precisely because it attends only to the mathematically modelable. Replying that science, unlike detectors, covers the whole of reality begs the question. The same fallacy underlies demands for metaphysics’ predictions — like asking for gardening’s metal-detecting record.
rubric: States the two-step argument accurately
Gives the metal-detector parody
Explains why success within a domain doesn’t show the domain is everything
Notes the question-begging reply

shortAnswer.q: Give Feser’s three objections to the view that the fundamental laws of nature are a brute fact.
shortAnswer.model: (1) It contradicts the principle of sufficient reason, defended in chapter 5. (2) It is ad hoc: its only motivation is to avoid arguments like the five proofs, since the Humean and quantum-mechanical challenges to PSR fail, and one can’t answer an offered explanation by saying there might be none (Gerson). (3) If the fundamental laws are unexplained, no higher-level law explains anything — like a shelf resting on brackets that are let go in midair. A regress of laws needs a self-explanatory terminus that imparts explanatory power without deriving it, which only something purely actual, simple, whose essence is existence, and necessary can be.
rubric: Conflict with PSR
Ad hoc / no independent motivation (Gerson point is a plus)
Higher-level laws lose explanatory power; shelf/brackets image
Connects to hierarchical series and a self-explanatory terminus

shortAnswer.q: Why does the objection that a designer would be more complex than the universe miss the five proofs?
shortAnswer.model: It targets Paley-style design arguments, which argue probabilistically from intricate, artifact-like complexity to a designer. The five proofs (1) don’t appeal to complexity in that sense — a pebble would do for the Neo-Platonic proof; (2) don’t appeal to probability — they are strict demonstrations about hierarchical causes operating now, so talk of a more parsimonious alternative misses them; and, most importantly, (3) agree that a complex cause would need a cause, which is precisely why they conclude that the first cause is absolutely simple. Nothing the atheist proposes as the terminus of explanation is simple in this way.
rubric: Identifies the target as design arguments (Paley/ID)
No appeal to complexity (pebble example)
Demonstration vs. probabilistic reasoning; hierarchical vs. linear
The proofs conclude to an absolutely simple cause — the key point

shortAnswer.q: Explain why Feser calls the “one god further” objection a category mistake, and why the point doesn’t depend on theism being true.
shortAnswer.model: The objection treats God as one member of the class “gods,” like Zeus or Thor. But the God of classical theism belongs to no genus (which would make him composite), shares no essence with others (which would distinguish his essence from existence), and is the purely actual source of all causal power — not a being but subsistent being itself. The pagan gods are limited beings with bodies, moods, parents, and beginnings. Treating God as one more god is like treating triangularity as one more triangle or the Form of the Good as one more good thing. Even if Euclid or Plato were wrong, Euclidean triangles would just be uninstantiated, not crooked; similarly, even if atheism were true, it wouldn’t be because God is one more nonexistent god.
rubric: States what the category mistake is
Gives at least two ways God differs from pagan gods (simplicity, essence = existence, pure act, not a being)
Uses the triangle or Form-of-the-Good analogy
Explains why the point holds whether or not theism is true

shortAnswer.q: How does Feser answer Mackie’s logical problem of evil?
shortAnswer.model: He offers a defense, not a theodicy. Mackie’s second premise — an omnipotent being faces no limits and a good being eliminates all the evil it can — fails twice. Omnipotence doesn’t extend to contradictions, so if some goods logically require evils, God can’t have the goods without them. And a good being doesn’t eliminate every evil it can, because some goods presuppose evils (the parent who won’t cancel homework). Against Mackie’s point that God could create free beings who always choose good, Feser grants it is possible, even with morally significant choices, but denies such a world could contain all the goods of ours: forgiveness and mercy require wrongdoing; courage requires danger; compassion requires misfortune; sacrifice requires loss. Mackie later conceded the logical argument fails.
rubric: Defense vs. theodicy
Omnipotence and contradictions
Goodness doesn’t require eliminating every evil (homework example)
Grants Mackie’s free-will point but cites goods that require evil
Mackie’s later concession (bonus)

shortAnswer.q: What is Rowe’s evidential argument and how does Feser respond?
shortAnswer.model: Rowe argues that a perfect being would prevent suffering preventable without losing a greater good or permitting something as bad; probably some suffering is like that (the fawn burned in a forest fire, suffering for days); so probably there is no such being. He concedes we can’t prove there is no greater good. Feser replies that believing there is no greater good is rational only if we lack independent reason to think a good God exists — and the proofs, plus the arguments for God’s attributes, supply it. Since Rowe grants a hidden good is possible, independent proof of God gives reason to think it actual. So the argument can’t challenge the proofs without first refuting them independently. Our ignorance is also expected: if there is an afterlife, an endless good could outweigh finite suffering, and we can no more grasp it than a child can grasp adulthood.
rubric: Accurately states Rowe’s argument and the fawn
Notes Rowe’s concession
Independent-evidence reply
The argument can’t challenge the proofs without refuting them first
Afterlife / child-adult point and that its possibility suffices for a defense

shortAnswer.q: Identify the two assumptions behind the divine hiddenness argument and summarize Feser’s case against each.
shortAnswer.model: (1) If God existed his existence would be obvious. Schellenberg grounds this in God’s desire for personal relationship, but not all theists hold that (Aristotle’s aloof Unmoved Mover), and even for those who do, the argument doesn’t touch the attributes the proofs establish. Regarding God’s love, as with evil, independent proof of a loving God implies there is a greater good in his not being more obvious. Hick’s epistemic distance is overstated but contains a kernel: finite minds and free will allow error. (2) God’s existence isn’t obvious to most people. In fact most people historically and today are theists of some kind; the weakness of ordinary people’s reasons no more makes God hidden than laymen’s weak grasp of science makes science hidden; most experts historically held God knowable by argument; and intellectuals who reject God on incompetent objections have no standing to call him hidden.
rubric: States both assumptions
Aristotle counterexample and limited scope of the argument
Greater-good reply parallel to Rowe
Hick’s epistemic distance and its kernel of truth
Most people are theists; layman-science analogy

shortAnswer.q: What does “demonstration” mean for classical theists, and why doesn’t widespread disagreement show that the proofs fail?
shortAnswer.model: A demonstration is a deductively valid argument from premises that are certain, their certainty shown by metaphysical analysis. It is more secure than scientific inference because it isn’t probabilistic or a best-explanation inference, and its premises can’t be overturned by future observation, since all observation presupposes them (any future experience would itself be a change). But nothing about such arguments implies everyone will immediately see their force, or that no hard work is needed to defend them. Disagreement doesn’t show failure: much criticism is ill-informed, and skeptics apply a double standard — arguments for materialism or against free will aren’t said to fail merely because they have critics (Putnam’s point). What a demonstration requires is that it can be defended against every objection.
rubric: Definition: valid deduction from certain premises
Two ways it differs from scientific inference
Change-example or equivalent
Controversy ≠ failure; double standard
Standard: defensible against all objections

shortAnswer.q: How would you respond, briefly and humanely, to a friend who says their suffering makes belief in God impossible?
shortAnswer.model: First, listen and acknowledge that what happened is truly evil — not secretly good. Admit honestly that you don’t know why it happened; Feser offers only a defense, not an explanation of particular evils, and argues we should expect not to see God’s reasons. If and when your friend wants to think it through, share gently that the reasons for believing in God don’t depend on explaining this event; that some of the deepest goods — mercy, courage, compassion — exist only where there is suffering; and that if God is real and good, this suffering is not the last word. Avoid clichés like “everything happens for a reason,” and don’t use their pain as a debate.
rubric: Listening and acknowledgment come first
Honest admission of not knowing why (defense, not theodicy)
Gentle statement of the core points only when welcome
Avoids glibness and clichés

shortAnswer.q: Explain the airplane-engineer analogy and use it to answer someone who says physics has shown that purposes don’t exist.
shortAnswer.model: Engineers calculating a plane’s capacity treat passengers as average weights, ignoring everything else. This is useful, but nobody concludes from their data that passengers have no meal or movie preferences; the data are silent because the method looked only at weight. Physics likewise attends only to what can be described mathematically, so qualities, meanings, and purposes are left out by design. Their absence from physics’ description is guaranteed by the method, not discovered. So “physics doesn’t mention purposes” gives no reason to think there are none.
rubric: Describes the analogy accurately
Identifies the method’s deliberate restriction
Distinguishes omission-by-method from discovery-of-absence
Applies it explicitly to purposes

shortAnswer.q: Explain the four theories of laws of nature Feser considers and why none makes laws the ultimate explanation.
shortAnswer.model: Aristotelian: laws describe how things act given their natures, so they presuppose the things and can’t explain their existence. Cartesian-Newtonian: laws express God’s ordering of the world, so God is the real explainer. Humean: laws summarize regularities, telling us that a pattern exists but not why — redescribing rather than explaining. Platonic: laws are abstract objects things participate in, but we’d still need to explain why a physical world participates in them and in these rather than others. On every view, something beyond the laws is needed, and denying that any ultimate explanation exists is a philosophical claim that violates PSR.
rubric: All four views stated correctly
The specific failure of each
Conclusion that explanation must go beyond laws/science
PSR point about “no ultimate explanation”

shortAnswer.q: Explain how Feser’s reply to divine hiddenness parallels his reply to Rowe’s evidential argument.
shortAnswer.model: In both cases the objection says a perfectly good God would not permit something — pointless suffering, or his own non-obviousness. And in both cases Feser answers that if we have independent proof that a good, loving, omnipotent, omniscient God exists, then we have reason to believe that whatever he permits serves a greater good, even if we cannot identify it. Schellenberg would have to show no such greater good is possible, which is no more plausible than claiming no good could come from Rowe’s fawn — something even Rowe concedes he can’t show. So neither argument threatens the proofs unless it first refutes them.
rubric: Identifies the shared structure
Independent-proof / greater-good reply
Rowe’s concession used against Schellenberg
Neither challenges the proofs without first refuting them

shortAnswer.q: Why does Feser think the charge that theistic arguments are rationalizations fails? Include his use of Thomas Nagel.
shortAnswer.model: First, it is an ad hominem fallacy — poisoning the well: whether an argument is good is independent of the arguer’s motives or character. Second, the charge cuts both ways: someone can want God not to exist and so avoid scrutinizing theistic arguments. Nagel candidly admitted he hopes there is no God and suspected this “cosmic authority problem” drives much scientism and reductionism. Feser adds that not all atheists (or theists) are dishonest; the point is that motives settle nothing, and only examining the arguments does.
rubric: Identifies poisoning the well / ad hominem
Symmetry of the charge
Nagel’s admission used correctly
Explicitly does not claim atheists are dishonest
Motives irrelevant — examine the arguments

shortAnswer.q: State the “God of the philosophers” objection and Feser’s two replies, including the atoms analogy.
shortAnswer.model: The objection: the simple, purely actual First Cause of the proofs isn’t the God ordinary believers pray to. Reply one: irrelevant even if true — if the proofs succeed, atheism is false, and what remains is a debate among theists about revelation. Reply two: false. Catholic teaching, for instance, holds that the God of the Bible is the God known by reason — omnipotence and omniscience knowable both ways, the Trinity only by revelation. And ordinary believers hold the same God in a less sophisticated way, just as a layman who pictures molecules as balls and sticks still believes in atoms.
rubric: Objection stated fairly
Irrelevance reply
Catholic reason/revelation example
Atoms analogy for the ordinary believer

shortAnswer.q: Scenario: in one conversation, a skeptic raises (a) “science is the only way to know things,” (b) “who designed the designer?”, and (c) “smart people reject your arguments.” Diagnose each using the three-part pattern and give a one-line answer to each.
shortAnswer.model: (a) Self-refuting: the claim isn’t something science could establish. One line: “Only science gives knowledge” isn’t a scientific discovery. (b) Attacks a caricature: it assumes God is complex, whereas the proofs conclude to an absolutely simple cause. One line: Agreed, a complex cause needs a cause — that’s why the proofs end in something with no parts. (c) Wrong standard: it treats controversy as refutation, a test no philosophical argument passes. One line: Every serious argument has critics; the question is whether their objections work.
rubric: Correct diagnosis of (a) as self-refuting
Correct diagnosis of (b) as caricature
Correct diagnosis of (c) as wrong standard
A crisp, accurate one-liner for each

A mind-independent objective world; law-like regularities in it; our intellect and senses can discover and describe them.

flashcards.front: Humean view of laws — why no ultimate explanation
flashcards.back: Laws merely summarize regularities: they say that a pattern holds, not why. They redescribe rather than explain.

Itself a philosophical, not scientific, claim — and false, since it violates PSR.

Searches for his keys only where the light is and concludes they can’t be anywhere else — the scientism mindset.

(1) Violates PSR; (2) ad hoc — motivated only by avoiding the proofs; (3) leaves higher-level laws with no real explanatory power.

Forgiveness and mercy (require wrongdoing), courage (danger), compassion (misfortune), sacrifice (loss of a good).

A fawn burned in a lightning-caused fire, suffering for days before dying — Rowe’s example of apparently pointless suffering.

Overstated (the world isn’t religiously ambiguous; believers do evil without doubting God), but a kernel of truth: finite minds and free will give us a long leash in what we think.
Rejecting an argument because of the arguer’s motives. Irrelevant to validity and soundness — and it cuts both ways (Nagel’s cosmic authority problem).
