flashcards.front: What does step 6 claim, and why?
flashcards.back: If “science” is stretched to include philosophy, natural theology counts too — since Aristotle and Aquinas regarded it as a science more certain than physics.

flashcards.front: What does step 9 claim, and why?
flashcards.back: Features a method leaves out by design aren’t shown to be absent — as the airplane engineers’ data say nothing about passengers’ tastes.

flashcards.front: What does step 11 claim, and why?
flashcards.back: Physics can’t describe all of reality and implies there is more — because it gives only structure (Russell), and structure must be the structure of something.

flashcards.front: What does step 13 claim, and why?
flashcards.back: On every theory of laws (Aristotelian, Cartesian-Newtonian, Humean, Platonic), laws can’t be the ultimate explanation — each view leaves something beyond the laws to be explained or does the explaining elsewhere.

flashcards.front: What does step 14 claim, and why?
flashcards.back: Ultimate explanation lies beyond science, and denying it is a philosophical claim that violates PSR.

flashcards.front: What does step 16 claim, and why?
flashcards.back: The argument from success is invalid — it has the same form as “metal detectors are most successful at finding metal, so only metal exists.”

flashcards.front: What does step 18 claim, and why?
flashcards.back: “Science or mere conceptual analysis” refutes itself (it’s neither) and logic and mathematics fit neither category — a version of Hume’s Fork.

flashcards.front: What does step 20 claim, and why?
flashcards.back: With scientism gone, the proofs must be met on their own terms: a false premise, invalid step, or begged question — they are demonstrations from what science presupposes.

flashcards.front: What does the concluding step (23) claim?
flashcards.back: No popular objection overturns the five proofs; the burden remains on the critic to engage the demonstrations themselves.
That claim isn’t something science discovered — so by its own rule you couldn’t know it.

flashcards.front: One-line reply: “Science’s success shows it’s the whole truth.”
flashcards.back: A metal detector’s perfect record doesn’t prove only metal exists.

flashcards.front: One-line reply: “You trust your cardiologist — you’re inconsistent.”
flashcards.back: Trusting a tool for its job isn’t believing it’s the only tool.

flashcards.front: One-line reply: “Science covers everything worth knowing.”
flashcards.back: Grading science only on the questions it’s built to answer guarantees a perfect score — and “only those matter” isn’t science.

flashcards.front: One-line reply: “Non-science is mere conceptual analysis.”
flashcards.back: That dichotomy is neither science nor conceptual analysis — it falls into the gap it denies exists.

flashcards.front: One-line reply: “The fundamental laws are a brute fact.”
flashcards.back: If the bottom law explains nothing, nothing resting on it explains anything either.
Agreed, a complex cause needs a cause — that’s why the proofs end in something with no parts.
Zeus is a being inside the world; God is the reason there’s a world — rejecting one isn’t a smaller version of rejecting the other.

flashcards.front: One-line reply: “The philosophers’ God isn’t the God people worship.”
flashcards.back: If the proofs work, atheism is false either way — and it’s one God known by different routes.

flashcards.front: One-line reply: Mackie’s logical problem of evil.
flashcards.back: Forgiveness, courage, and compassion can’t exist where there’s nothing to forgive, fear, or pity — so evil and a good God aren’t contradictory.
“I can’t see a reason” becomes “there is none” only if you lack independent reason to trust the one who can see.
If God is hidden from most people, most people haven’t noticed.
Why someone gives an argument tells you nothing about whether it’s sound.

flashcards.front: One-line reply: “It can’t be a proof — people disagree.”
flashcards.back: Every major philosophical argument has critics; the question is whether their objections work.
Science: powerful methods for the measurable. Scientism: the philosophical thesis that only those methods yield knowledge — not itself scientific.
Controversial = has critics. Failed = actually has a false premise, invalid step, or begs the question. Only the second defeats a demonstration.

flashcards.front: Distinction: crude understanding vs. different object
flashcards.back: The layman’s ball-and-stick atoms are still atoms; the ordinary believer’s untechnical God is still the God of the philosophers.

flashcards.front: Why Aristotle’s Unmoved Mover matters for the hiddenness debate
flashcards.back: It contemplates itself and ignores us — so Schellenberg’s premise that God must seek relationship isn’t true of every theism, and his argument isn’t fully general.

teachBack:
**Challenge:** Explain to a science-minded friend who has never read Feser why “science doesn’t need God” is not an argument against the five proofs — in under four minutes, without using the words “metaphysics,” “Aristotelian,” or “actuality.”

You must: (1) separate science from scientism in one sentence; (2) use either the metal detector or the airplane engineers; (3) show why “only science gives knowledge” can’t be proved by science; and (4) finish by naming the one thing that *would* count against a proof (a false premise or an invalid step).

**Round two:** In two minutes each, give a one-line answer and a one-paragraph explanation for “Who designed the designer?” and “You’re an atheist about Zeus — just go one god further.” Use no analogy twice.

**Round three (the hard one):** Role-play with a partner who plays someone whose close relative has recently died. Your goal is *not* to win. Practice listening, acknowledging, saying “I don’t know why,” and only then — if your partner invites it — explaining the difference between a defense and a theodicy and why some goods require evil. Ask your partner afterward: did anything I said feel glib?

**Check yourself:** Could your friend now restate the scientism dilemma in their own words? Did you ever accidentally argue from a gap in current science? Did you claim to know why God permits a particular evil? If yes to either of the last two, revisit the summary sections on scientism’s problems and on Mackie and Rowe.
videoPrompt: Audience: thoughtful beginners, including skeptics raised on popular science. Overview the second half of Chapter 7 of Feser’s Five Proofs. Emphasize, in order: (1) scientism — only science gives knowledge — is self-refuting or empty, and physics captures measurable structure by design (airplane engineers treating passengers as average weights; the metal detector); (2) brute-fact laws explain nothing, like a shelf whose brackets are let go in midair; (3) “who designed the designer?” and “one god further” attack a caricature: the proofs reach an absolutely simple God who is being itself, not one more god (triangle vs. triangularity); (4) evil: defense vs. theodicy, goods like forgiveness and courage that require evil, Rowe’s fawn; (5) hiddenness, motives, disagreement. Correct two myths: rejecting scientism means rejecting science; Feser claims to know why each evil happens. Tone: warm, clear, fair to critics, humane about suffering.

readingGuide.beforeYouRead:
These are the last thirty-five pages of the book, and they’re among the easiest to read, because Feser stops building arguments and starts answering the objections you have probably heard yourself: “science is the only way to know things,” “who designed the designer?”, “you’re an atheist about Zeus, just go one god further,” “why does God allow suffering?”, “why doesn’t God make himself obvious?”

The first stretch (pages 273–285) is the hardest and most important. Feser takes on **scientism**, the idea that science is the only real source of knowledge. He cares about it because it’s the hidden reason many people never look at arguments for God: if only science counts, philosophical arguments can be ignored. You don’t have to know any science or philosophy to follow him. His examples are everyday ones: airplane engineers, metal detectors, a drunk looking for his keys, a student who takes only easy classes.

The rest of the chapter goes through one objection at a time, each under its own heading in quotation marks. Every reply uses the same toolkit. Feser shows that the objection refutes itself, or that it attacks a picture of God the proofs don’t defend (one more complicated being in the universe), or that it holds arguments for God to a standard no one uses elsewhere.

The pages on suffering (294–300) are the most emotionally serious. Pay attention to how modest Feser’s claim is. He doesn’t say he knows why any particular evil happens. He argues only that evil and a good God aren’t contradictory, and that not seeing God’s reasons is exactly what we should expect.

He sometimes refers back to earlier chapters: the principle of sufficient reason (chapter 5), divine simplicity (chapters 2 and 6), and the idea that God is existence itself (chapter 4). This module’s key-terms list explains each one, so you can read the chapter even if you haven’t mastered those chapters yet. If a sentence sounds technical, keep going. The main point of each section is almost always stated plainly in its first and last paragraphs.

knowFirst.plain: The belief that science is the only way to really know anything. Feser argues against the belief, not against science.
The idea that everything has an explanation, either in itself or in something else. Feser defended it earlier in the book and relies on it here.
The classical idea that God has no parts of any kind. It explains why God isn’t a “complex designer” and isn’t one god among many.
The idea that God isn’t one more thing that exists but is existence itself, the source of everything else’s existence.
An argument whose conclusion follows necessarily from certain starting points, as opposed to a best guess or a probability estimate.
The claim that all knowledge is either true by definition or learned by observation. Feser shows the claim itself is neither.
Showing that evil and God aren’t contradictory, without claiming to know why God allows any particular evil.
An attempt to explain why God actually allows evil. Feser mostly doesn’t try to give one here.
Treating something as the wrong kind of thing, like treating triangularity as one more triangle.
Dismissing an argument because of the arguer’s motives instead of checking whether it is sound.

questionsToHold: Is the claim “only science gives knowledge” something science could ever show?
When physics leaves something out of its description, has it shown that the thing isn’t real, or just that it wasn’t looking for it?
Does each objection attack the God the five proofs actually conclude to, a simple and purely actual source of all being, or a different picture of God?
Is each objection judging the proofs as demonstrations, or as probability guesses, or by who is arguing?
On suffering: how much is Feser claiming to know, and how much is he deliberately not claiming?
What would it take to actually refute one of the five proofs?

map.section: “Science is the only genuine source of knowledge…” — the four problems; problem 1 (self-refuting or trivial)
map.what: Feser defines scientism, lists four problems with it, and argues the first: the claim that only science gives knowledge isn’t scientific, and science depends on philosophy. Stretching “science” to include philosophy makes the claim empty and lets natural theology in.
map.tip: The dilemma (self-refuting or trivial) is the key. Slow down at the list of science’s presuppositions and at the Aristotle/Aquinas point about natural theology as a science.

map.section: Problem 2: science can’t give a complete description of reality
map.what: Physics describes only what can be put into mathematics. The airplane engineers show that what a method leaves out isn’t thereby shown to be unreal. Russell’s point is that physics gives structure but not what has the structure.
map.tip: The engineers example is easy. Reread the Russell paragraph and the sentence after it about structure needing something that has the structure.

map.section: Problem 3: laws of nature can’t be the ultimate explanation
map.what: A survey of four views of what laws are (Aristotelian, Descartes–Newton, Humean, Platonic), showing that on none of them can laws explain why anything exists.
map.tip: Make a four-row table: view, what a law is, why it can’t be ultimate. This is the most abstract stretch; the ending (the appeal to PSR) is short but important.

map.what: Why science’s success doesn’t show it covers all of reality: the metal detector, the cardiologist charge, gardening and spatulas, and the drunk under the streetlamp.
map.tip: Enjoyable and quick. Pay attention to Feser’s two-line reconstruction of Rosenberg’s argument and his parody of it.

map.section: Fallbacks: “worth knowing,” conceptual analysis, Hume’s Fork, logic and mathematics
map.what: Two retreats from scientism fail. The easy-A student and the self-refuting fork show why, and logic and mathematics are knowledge that is neither science nor wordplay. The section ends with the thief and the squad car.
map.tip: Test Hume’s Fork on itself as you read. Footnote 46 (neuroscience) is worth reading. The passage on logic and mathematics connects to chapter 3.

map.section: “The fundamental laws of nature are best regarded as an unexplained brute fact…”
map.what: Three problems with saying the deepest laws have no explanation: it violates PSR, it is ad hoc, and it leaves every law explaining nothing (the shelf on brackets let go in midair).
map.tip: The third problem is the deep one. Connect it to the hand-stick-stone series from chapter 1.

map.section: “A designer of the universe would be even more complex…”
map.what: Why the Hume and Dawkins objection misses: the proofs aren’t design arguments, don’t rely on probability, and agree that complex things need causes, which is why they conclude to a simple God.
map.tip: Note the pebble example and the phrase “most importantly” introducing the third reply.

map.section: “Anyone who rejects Zeus, Venus, Thor… go one god further”
map.what: Feser gives two replies. There are arguments for God and none for Zeus, and more deeply, God isn’t a member of the category “gods” at all. The anti-Euclidean and anti-Platonist analogies illustrate the category mistake.
map.tip: Read the list of how pagan gods differ from the classical God slowly. The paragraph beginning “Notice that the point has nothing to do with whether…” is subtle; reread it.

map.section: “The God of philosophical theism is not the God most ordinary religious believers believe in.”
map.what: The objection is irrelevant even if true, since atheism would still be false. It is also false: some religions identify the two, and ordinary believers hold the same God less technically, like the ball-and-stick picture of atoms.
map.tip: Short and clear. Note the example of reason and revelation (omnipotence vs. the Trinity).

map.section: “The reality of suffering and of other kinds of evil shows that God does not exist” — defense vs. theodicy; Mackie
map.what: Feser distinguishes defense from theodicy and answers Mackie’s logical argument. Omnipotence excludes contradictions, and a good being doesn’t remove every evil. He grants Mackie’s free-will point but argues that forgiveness, mercy, courage, and compassion require evil.
map.tip: Read footnotes 50 (the two meanings of “theodicy”) and 54 (not the best possible world). Notice where Feser declines to follow Plantinga.

map.section: The evidential argument (Rowe) and the afterlife
map.what: Rowe’s fawn, and Feser’s reply that independent proof of a good God gives reason to believe in unseen goods. Then the afterlife point: an endless good, and a child’s view of adulthood.
map.tip: Slow down at the paragraph beginning “The problem with Rowe’s argument…” and trace why Rowe’s own concession matters. Keep in mind that this is a defense, not a claim to know God’s reasons.

map.section: “If God really existed, then he would not be ‘hidden’ from us…”
map.what: Divine hiddenness. Feser challenges both assumptions (God would be obvious; he isn’t), weighs Hick’s epistemic distance, and argues that most people have never found God hidden.
map.tip: Label the two assumptions in the margin before reading. The list of things philosophers have denied is a memorable aside.

map.section: “Arguments for God’s existence are just rationalizations…”
map.what: Poisoning the well, and Thomas Nagel’s admission that he hopes there is no God.
map.tip: Quick. Notice that Feser explicitly says not all atheists are dishonest.

map.section: “No one can claim to have a proof or demonstration that God exists…”
map.what: Three replies. The criticism is often uninformed, there is a double standard (Putnam), and critics misunderstand what a demonstration is. The book ends with Q.E.D.
map.tip: Read footnote 65 (Putnam). The paragraph on why the premise “change occurs” can’t be overturned is a good summary of the whole book’s method.

afterReading: Without looking, state the dilemma for scientism in two sentences.
Explain the airplane-engineers example and the metal-detector argument to an imaginary friend, then say what each proves and what it doesn’t.
For each of the nine objection headings, write a one-line reply, then check it against this module’s objection list.
Sort the objections into three groups: self-refuting, attacks a caricature, uses the wrong standard. Where does the problem of evil fit, and why is it harder to sort?
Explain the difference between a defense and a theodicy, and why Feser offers only a defense.
Say what a “demonstration” is and why disagreement doesn’t show a proof has failed.
Take the module’s quiz and the section checks, then reread any section where you missed more than one question.
